bio.en: Lane Shackleton is the Chief Product Officer at Coda, where he has led product for over eight years, and previously was a Group Product Manager at YouTube.
bio.zh: 莱恩·沙克尔顿（Lane Shackleton）是 Coda 的首席产品官，已在产品岗位深耕八年多，此前是 YouTube 的产品组经理。

summary.en: Lane argues you should actively seek "oh shit" moments - situations where you feel unqualified - because that's where real growth happens. He reframes the common "are you growing?" question into "how many stretch moments have you had lately?" The episode offers career advice on leaning into discomfort and building a foundation for the next level.
summary.zh: 莱恩认为，你应当主动去寻找"糟了"时刻——那些让你觉得自己不够格的处境——因为真正的成长就在那里发生。他把常见的"你在成长吗？"这个问题，重构为"最近你经历了多少次被拉伸的时刻？"。本期提供了关于拥抱不适感、为下一阶段打下基础的职业建议。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Moments that stretch you or moments that you feel uncomfortable in or you find yourself saying, "Oh shit. I shouldn't be here," or, "I'm under qualified to be here," those are the moments you should be seeking out. Those are the moments that stretch you and give you a new foundation. So oftentimes you'll hear a career question like, "Hey, do you feel like you're growing in your role?" And that's a very ambiguous, in my opinion, way to ask this question. A much sharper way is like, "Hey, how many, oh shit moments have you had in the last six months, year, two years, and what are they?" I think if you ask yourself that question and the answer is, "It's been a really long time since I've been stretched in some meaningful way or I've felt like I'm under qualified to be there," then it may be worth digging into.
turns.zh:
那些能让你成长的时刻，那些让你感到不适的时刻，或者那些让你忍不住说出“天啊，我不该来这里”或者“我根本不够格来这里”的时刻——这些才是你应该主动寻找的时刻。它们能拓展你的能力边界，为你奠定新的发展基础。  

所以你常会听到这样一个职业发展问题：“嘿，你觉得自己在现有职位上成长了吗？” 但在我看来，这种提问方式太模糊了。更尖锐一点的问法应该是：“嘿，过去六个月、一年、两年里，你经历过多少次‘天啊，我不该来这里’的时刻？它们都是些什么情况？” 我认为，如果你问自己这个问题，答案是“很久没有经历过真正意义上的挑战成长了，或者总觉得自己不够格胜任当前职位”，那么就值得深挖一下了。

turns.en: Amazing. Okay. So on that same topic, I noticed maybe your first job was a mountain guide in Alaska. Was that inspired by this legacy? And also why did you decide not to pursue that and get into product management? Completely different life.

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. Very, very different. Very different time. Didn't have kids back then. I think I was convinced at the time I wanted a career outside. Just loved spending time in the mountains and climbing, things like that. To be honest, I wasn't the best guide. There were a lot of amazing guides out there that just had ... They were almost invincible in terms of their ability to climb for 20, 30 hours. But I learned a lot from the experience and maybe the quick story on why I stopped guiding. I was on what is a dream trip for mountain guides, which is we were flown to a remote portion of southeast Alaska. It's an hour long flight. Mountain called Mount Fairweather. Beautiful 15,000 foot peak. And as a part of climbing on glaciers one of the things that you do for context is you're roped to another person. And the reason that you do that is because if someone falls in a crevasse, you want to be able to stop them or pull them out. (00:06:48): So I was roped to a very nice client that I was guiding and he fell pretty close to the top on our way down. And luckily we were able to self-arrest and arrest that fall. But I spent probably the next six hours walking down that mountain thinking the same thing over and over again, which is I really don't want to die roped to someone that I barely know and don't trust or love. So that was the last season that I guided. But tons of great memories and learnings and I think it impacted my life in a pretty significant way.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。完全不同。当时的时代也不同。当时我还没有孩子。我记得当时坚信自己想走出户外。只是喜欢在山里攀岩之类的活动。说实话，我当时不是个出色的向导。那里有很多优秀的向导，他们几乎无所畏惧，能连续攀爬20、30个小时。但我从那段经历中学到了很多。或许我可以快速讲讲为什么我不再做向导了。那是我作为登山向导最梦幻的一次经历——我们被空运到阿拉斯加东南部一个偏远地区，飞行时间一个小时。那里有一座叫费尔韦瑟山的山峰，海拔15000英尺，景色壮美。在攀登冰川时，为了安全，队员们通常会用绳子连接。原因是如果有人掉进裂缝，你得尽力阻止他们，或者把他们拉出来。（00:06:48）当时我正和一位客户用绳子连接，他在下山途中离山顶很近的地方掉下去了。幸运的是，我们成功用自制制动器阻止了他的坠落。但接下来的六个小时，我在下山的路上反复思考同一个问题：我真的不想和一个几乎不认识、既不信任也不喜欢的人用绳子连接着等死。所以那是我最后一个向导季。但那里有很多美好的回忆和收获，我觉得这段经历对我的生活影响深远。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Damn. Software much lower stakes. I guess just while we're on this topic, is there any parallels or big lesson you learned from that experience that you bring to product?
turns.zh: 天啊。软件开发的风险要小得多。我想既然我们已经谈到这个话题，你从那段经历中得到的任何启发或重要教训，是否能应用到产品开发中呢？

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: One is just preparation. I think when you go climbing or when you guide climbing, you spend months and months preparing for usually a few days of climbing. So there's that kind of preparation. There's also just a million checklists. So before you go on an expedition, you may check a checklist of all your equipment, stuff like that a dozen times or more. So you ensure redundancy across all your systems. So that was definitely a parallel. The other thing I think about a lot is just how to stay calm in challenging or scary scenarios. We had another instance where I had a client pull a big chunk of rock off and break their feet and I was the junior guide on that particular instance and the more senior guide looked at me, looked at the situation and was like, "Okay, we're getting this guy out of here right now." Put him on his back and we basically took turns carrying him out for a couple miles I'll just never forget instances like that where the clarity of stay calm, assess the situation, prioritize, take action. There's a mini version of that when you're building software, I think. So experiences like that, I think, even though I only did it for a handful of summers, were pretty profound.
turns.zh: 首先是充分准备。我觉得无论是攀岩还是担任向导，通常你需要花数月时间准备，却往往只需几天攀岩。所以这就是充分准备的意义。还有无数份检查清单。比如在探险前，你可能会反复检查所有装备清单十几次甚至更多次，以确保所有系统都具备冗余。这绝对是两个相似的方面。另外，我经常思考如何在挑战性或恐怖场景中保持冷静。我们曾遇到过这样的情况：有位客户被掉落的大石头砸伤脚。我当时是初级向导，资深向导看着我，审视了整个局面，然后说道："好，我们现在就把他带出去。"把他背在背上，我们轮流抬着他走了好几英里。我永远忘不了那样的时刻——保持冷静、评估形势、分清轻重缓急、采取行动。这些能力在软件开发中也有小版本的体现。虽然我只做了几个夏天的向导，但这些经历确实意义深远。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. What a very different life that life path would've been.
turns.zh: 是啊。如果走上那条人生道路，生活会截然不同。

turns.zh: 天哪。所以你提到了写作，你说这是你想写作的方向。回到我们聊天的核心话题，很明显你花了大量时间研究优秀产品经理和团队的运作方式。你写了很多关于优秀产品管理原则和团队仪式的文章。所以我想花大量时间从你的学习中提取尽可能多的精华，让听众也能受益。基本上，优秀产品经理的原则是什么，优秀团队的仪式又有哪些？一般来说，最优秀的团队是如何运作的？我的第一个问题是，你为什么开始做这些研究？是什么促使你投入如此多的时间和精力，去理解最优秀的团队和个人是如何运作的？

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. I've been asking myself that question a little bit lately. There's a few reasons. One reason is I just found myself giving a similar set of advice in one on ones. And so I think anytime you find as a leader yourself repeating the same lessons, it should be a good flag to say like, oh, I should probably scale this in some way. And as you know, as soon as you write something down, you have to clarify your own thinking and so it becomes very useful for that. And I don't think I quite expected how useful it would be in that sense. Writing something down and then putting it out there, you start to get feedback back of where you might've been right or where you might not be right. And so for me it's been a good learning experience there as well. I think the second reason is I've always been pretty frustrated with career ladders. Most companies have career ladders with 10 or 15 levels and as soon as they hit some scale levels, there's levels between levels and I feel like I looked at the one at Google and you needed a PhD to decipher it and interpret how to operate within it. (00:11:11): And so that's one piece of the construct. If you think more broadly though, they aren't consistent across companies, so now you're in a situation where you're in your version of the rat race. And so I found that I basically wanted to have a broader set of principles that transcended level. So things that could be true when you are an ICPM starting your career and things that can also be true when you're the head of product or running a product team or things like that. That's one. I won't rant further on that but I think that's one piece of it. (00:11:49): And then I think the last reason I'll mention is I was pretty inspired by a talk that is by this guy named Brett Victor, who's like a prototyper thinker. May have heard of his work. He has this talk called Inventing on Principle. And in the early days of Coda, one of our first designers, this guy Jeremy Britten, showed this talk to the company and my mind was blown. And I think it was one of those examples of someone developing a clear view of what principles they should operate with and then following that principle. And it was just a meta example of how important it is and how impactful it can be when you decide on a principle and then follow it. And so ever since then I've been thinking what are my principles as it pertains to building software and other things. So those are the three reasons that led me to start writing these things down.
turns.zh:
是啊，是啊。我最近也一直在问自己这个问题。原因有几个。首先，我发现自己在一对一沟通中反复给出相似的建议。所以我觉得，当你作为领导者发现自己在重复讲同样的道理时，就应该警醒了，应该反思一下：哦，我或许需要用某种方式把这件事系统化。正如你们所知，一旦把想法写下来，你就必须理清自己的思路，所以这真的很有帮助。我没想到它在这种情况下会如此有效。把想法写下来，然后公开分享，你就能得到反馈，知道自己哪些地方做对了，哪些地方可能做得不够。这对我来说也是一次很好的学习经历。  

第二个原因是我对职场晋升阶梯一直很不满。大多数公司都有10到15个晋升级别，但一旦达到某个级别，级别之间又会出现层级划分。我记得看过谷歌的晋升阶梯，简直需要博士学位才能理解和遵循其中的规则。（00:11:11）这就是现有晋升体系的一个缩影。如果从更宏观的角度看，这些体系在不同公司并不一致，所以你会陷入一种无休止的内卷竞争。于是我发现自己其实更希望有一套超越级别限制的通用原则。这些原则既适用于刚入职的ICPM工程师，也适用于产品负责人，或者管理产品团队的人。这就是第一个原因。我就不多说了，但我认为这很重要。  

（00:11:49）最后一个原因是我被Brett Victor的一次演讲深深启发。他是一位原型设计师，可能你们听说过他的作品。他有一场名为《基于原则的创新》的演讲。在Coda早期阶段，我们公司的首位设计师Jeremy Britten向全公司推荐了这场演讲，我深受震撼。这是他清晰阐述应遵循的原则，并据此行动的典范。这让我深刻意识到，当你确定一个原则并坚持执行时，其重要性和影响力是多么巨大。从那以后，我一直在思考在软件开发等领域，我的原则应该是什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. We're going to find that talk and link to it in the show notes. I want to ask about what principles you've come to, but I also want to understand how you actually ended up doing ladders and performance review stuff at Coda. Would it be better to talk about that later after we go through some of these things or is there something you want to share first of just how you think about it at Coda?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们会找到那场演讲，并在节目笔记中附上链接。我想问问你得出了哪些原则，但我也想了解你如何在Coda引入晋升阶梯和绩效评估体系的。是等我们讨论完这些内容后再谈这个话题更好，还是你现在就想分享一下你在Coda的思考？

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: When we were doing career ladders, first of all, we put it off for quite a bit of time and that was based on the advice of a lot of other leaders that said as soon as you introduce this, then the incentives flip from being company focused to being individual focused. So I think we delayed it for a good bit of time. There came a time where we decided, "Hey look, we really do need to provide better guidance here about what it means to grow and what it means to be great." And so about the same time we were doing the levels thing I started writing down some of the principles that I've been publishing. One of the things that I think about a lot when talking about levels is just how to keep everyone oriented toward their team and their company. And I think that we've done a really good job of that over the years. So levels aren't by any means at the forefront of any company discussion. In fact, we don't use titles that much.
turns.zh: 谈到职业晋升阶梯时，首先我们拖延了很久。这是基于许多其他领导者的建议，他们认为一旦引入这个体系，激励机制就会从以公司为导向转向以个人为导向。因此，我们推迟了很久。直到某个时刻，我们决定：“嘿，看吧，我们确实需要在这里提供更好的指导，说明成长意味着什么，卓越又意味着什么。” 大约在我们制定晋升阶梯的同时， 我开始写下一些我一直在发布的原则。谈到晋升阶梯时，我经常思考的一个问题是如何让每个人都专注于自己的团队和公司。我认为我们多年来在这方面做得非常出色。因此，晋升阶梯绝不是任何公司讨论的核心问题。事实上，我们不常使用职位头衔。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You said that it's not specific to role. Do you mean the same leveling attributes are the same from design and product and engineering?
turns.zh: 你说这不受角色限制。你的意思是设计、产品和工程部门的晋升标准是相同的吗？

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: We basically have five levels and we call them role stages and they go from apprentice to principal. So apprentice is ... Rope analogy here is learns about rope. Practitioner is can tie basic knots, shown complex knots. Given a problem, they can do it. Career is you can calculate rope strength. You know a lot about knots. Principal is basically invented nylon. So the bar is really, really high for principal in these levels and I think that that's appropriate. It should be aspirational that the bar is exceptionally high at the highest level of our role stages. I find it's a pretty good process to draw maybe a little bit of contrast with other companies. I think most other companies, especially large companies have 10 to 15 levels. I think we've made a really conscious choice to have only five. I think the other bit of contrast I would draw is basically role stages are not visible across the whole company. We're not showing levels of any individual PM or designer, and that's partially because we just don't want to put a big focus on it. And then probably the biggest difference is we have a centralized compensation committee and that's who decides compensation and so it's not the manager that drives your compensation. So those are some differences.
turns.zh: 我们基本上有五个级别，我们称之为角色阶段，从学徒到首席。学徒阶段……用绳子打比方的话，就是学习绳子的知识。从业者阶段是能够系基本结，展示复杂结。给他们一个问题，他们就能解决。职业阶段是能够计算绳子的强度。他们对结非常了解。首席阶段基本上是发明尼龙。因此，首席阶段的标准非常高，这很合适。在我们角色阶段的最高层级，标准极高，这应该是令人向往的。我发现将我们与其他公司进行对比是一个很好的过程。我认为大多数其他公司，特别是大型公司有10到15个级别。我们有意识地选择只有五个级别。我认为另一个不同之处是，角色阶段在整个公司内不公开。我们不会展示任何产品经理或设计师的级别，这部分是因为我们不想过度关注它。最大的不同可能是我们有一个中央薪酬委员会，由他们决定薪酬，而不是由经理来设定薪酬。这些就是一些不同之处。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Super cool. I've never seen it done this way before. I think it's an awesome example of first principles thinking, which I see a lot come out from your product team. And then just to make sure I heard you right, these five stages are roughly the same across role, so designers have the same five and they're described similarly.
turns.zh: 太酷了。我以前从未见过这样的做法。我认为这是第一性原理思维的一个很好的例子，我经常从你们的产品团队看到这种思维。然后为了确认我是否理解正确，这五个阶段在不同角色中大致相同吗？

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: That's right. They're described similarly at a high level, but then the specifics if you get into it are a little bit different.
turns.zh: 没错。高层面描述相似，但具体细节有所不同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I'm going to ask about what the principles are, or a few of them that you can share. But one other very tactical question. At what size of product teams, say just PMs, did you start to develop this framework?
turns.zh: 好的。我想问问这些原则是什么，或者你能分享几个。但还有一个非常实际的问题。在多大的产品团队规模下，比如仅限产品经理，你们开始开发这个框架？

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: We were probably at 20-ish PMs and designers when we did that.
turns.zh: 我们大概有20名左右的产品经理和设计师时做的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. So let me just ask, what are some of these principles you've narrowed it on as principles of great product managers?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，我再问问，你总结出的这些原则中，哪些是优秀产品经理的原则？

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Maybe it's helpful to start with a little higher level context on the unifying thesis. I think the unifying thesis is the core job of a product person in general is to turn ambiguity into clarity. And if you think about the job of a product leader or a product manager, everything is ambiguous all the time. It's like what's my role on this team? What problem are we solving? Who's the target customer? What prototype is going to solve this particular problem? So it's literally everything. And so if you're going to do the job well, you really need to get good at spotting ambiguity and turning it into clarity. And so the obvious question that follows from that is okay, great, that sounds like a great Hallmark card, but how do you actually do that? And so I think the principles that I've been writing down are very personal. They're my take on how to do this. (00:17:41): So the first one that I wrote about was systems not goals. And one of the ways that I started this post ... I'm a big fan of getting inspiration from outside of tech and so one of the stories that I tell is basically the story of Jerry Seinfeld. If you haven't seen the documentary Comedian, it's amazing, it's definitely worth watching. But the story goes, he's done Seinfeld the show and he's got all this material from the last 15 years and he comes in one day and he says, "Look, I'm going to throw away all my material and I'm going to start fresh." And this is unheard of in comedy for someone to just throw away all their old material and start fresh. And so the question is what does he do next? And the thing that he does is he sets a goal, which is basically to build up to an hour of material again. (00:18:34): But the goal isn't that important. What's important here is the system. So the system that he uses is he writes for an hour every morning, doesn't write for more if he doesn't want to, and then he goes and performs at night. And so when you rinse and repeat that system, do it hundreds of times, that's how he builds up from five minutes to 15 minutes to 30 minutes of material. And so I think that I take a lot of inspiration from that and I think product people can generally, which is instead of being obsessed with the goal, be obsessed with the system that gets you there. And so the phrase I sometimes use is goals with good intentions don't work. I really need to give a common example. A really common example is teams that are trying to learn about customers or do research. And one thing I've observed is a team may have a goal like an OKR of talking to 10 customers this quarter and they may or may not hit that OKR. And then if you watch closely, the next quarter, they may not have a goal of talking to customers anymore. And so their learning is going up and down. (00:19:49): And to draw a contrast, that's just really different than a team that has some default on system for talking to customers. Every few times a week they're talking to customers for whatever reason. And the impact of that is really hard to see until you understand that the latter team tends to have really good product instincts or really good customer instincts. It's because they've just had this default on mindset of talking to customers. And in the early days of Coda, we actually did something similar. We had a time allotted on Fridays and it was basically, it was on the calendar a customer or a potential customer was coming in and so you knew that it was going to happen and you had to have something to show. And so sometimes we'd be scrambling the three hours before to have a prototype ready for a customer. Sometimes we would've had something that we've been baking for a while. But the point is that it was default on. And so the way that we developed good customer instincts was not the goal, it was really just the system behind it. So that's one that I'm passionate about and I think it also translates into a lot of the rituals that we talk a lot about.
turns.zh:
或许先从更宏观的角度来理解统一论点会更有帮助。我认为产品经理的核心职责是化解模糊性。而当你审视产品负责人或产品经理的工作时，会发现模糊性无处不在。比如：我在团队中的角色是什么？我们要解决什么问题？目标客户是谁？哪个原型能解决特定问题？这些都是日常面临的困惑。若想做好这份工作，就必须善于识别模糊性并将其化解为清晰思路。

接下来自然会产生疑问：这听起来不错，但具体该怎么做？我总结的原则都源于个人实践，代表我对这项工作的理解。（00:17:41）第一个原则是关注系统而非目标。启发我写下这篇文章的灵感来源于科技领域之外——我非常推崇从其他领域汲取灵感。我常提到的例子是杰瑞·宋飞（Jerry Seinfeld）的故事。若你看过纪录片《喜剧演员》（Comedian），会发现他在《宋飞正传》（Seinfeld）完结后，将过去15年的素材全部丢弃，重新开始。这在喜剧界实属罕见。随后，他设定了一个目标——重新积累一小时的素材。（00:18:34）但目标本身并不重要，关键在于背后的系统。他遵循的系统是：每天早上写作一小时，若无灵感则停止，晚上进行表演。通过反复践行这个系统，他将素材从五分钟逐步扩展至15分钟、30分钟。

我从中汲取了深刻启示：与其执着于目标，不如专注于能达成目标的系统。举个常见例子：团队试图通过OKR（目标与关键结果）来了解客户，但结果往往喜忧参半。若仔细观察，下季度他们可能不再设定客户访谈目标。这种学习曲线起伏不定。

相比之下，建立系统化客户沟通机制的团队则截然不同。他们每周都会定期与客户交流，形成固定习惯。这种习惯的价值往往难以量化，但其背后的客户洞察力或产品直觉却显而易见。在Coda初期，我们也实施过类似策略：每周五固定时间段，日程表上标注有客户或潜在客户到访，团队必须准备好原型展示。为此，我们常在前三小时紧急赶工。
客户。有时我们会推出一些研发了很久的产品。但关键在于，这些产品必须是优质的。所以，培养优秀的客户洞察力并非最终目标，真正重要的是背后的系统支持。这正是我深感兴趣的地方，我认为这也体现在我们经常提及的诸多经营准则中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's so many directions I can go with this. I really like this one. It reminds me of something I did at Airbnb where we had a lunch with a host every Friday with the team and we had a community person find someone in San Francisco that's a host. And there's no agenda, it's just let's have lunch and meet the team. Curious what you're wondering.
turns.zh: 关于这个话题，我能想到很多方向。我特别喜欢这个主意。它让我想起在Airbnb的经历——每周五我们团队都会和房东共进午餐，由社区人员在旧金山为我们寻找房东。没有固定议程，就是一起吃午餐、认识团队成员。我很好奇你对此有什么看法。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And Airbnb hosts are always so nice and has such a pleasant experience. Also makes me think about this book, The Score Takes Care of Itself.
turns.zh: Airbnb的房东们总是非常友善，相处体验很棒。这也让我想起那本《得分自然》（The Score Takes Care of Itself）。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 对啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Have you read that?
turns.zh: 你读过这本书吗？

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 读过。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Where it's just do the fundamentals and you'll win?
turns.zh: 就是专注基本功，然后胜利自然而然？

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other thing it reminds me of is I have this quote hanging in my office here. I Believe it's from the Rick Rubin book. And the quote is, "The object isn't to make art, it's to be in that wonderful state which makes art inevitable."
turns.zh: 另外，我办公室里挂着里克·鲁宾（Rick Rubin）的书中的一句话：“目标不是创造艺术，而是处于那种让艺术自然发生的状态。”

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: I love it.
turns.zh: 我超爱这句话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like you just changed art-
turns.zh: 我感觉你刚刚把艺术重新定义了——

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Yeah. Rick Rubin's amazing.
turns.zh: 对啊，里克·鲁宾太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my god, it's so good. Just every section is this quotable thing I want ... I need to hold onto this thing.
turns.zh: 天哪，这本书太棒了。每一章都引人入胜，让我迫切想保留这些金句。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Yeah. He's got a great thing on listening. I really admire what he says about listening and I think that a lot of PMs could take that lesson, which is-
turns.zh: 是啊。他关于倾听的论述很棒。我很钦佩他对倾听的见解，我觉得很多产品经理都能从中汲取经验，比如——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. What is that lesson?
turns.zh: 对。具体是什么经验？

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: The way he talks about it is essentially you want to listen and absorb every fragment of what that person is saying, including their body language and everything else, and try to turn off the side which is crafting your response or figuring out what you're going to say next or what the problem with their argument is or whatever. It's quite hard to do. Because your default mode is always the next step of the conversation. But I think if you can really challenge yourself, like he says, to pause and really try to internalize holistically what that person's saying, it's pretty powerful.
turns.zh: 他的核心观点是，你要全神贯注地吸收对方传达的每一丝信息，包括他们的肢体语言和其他细节，暂时关闭自己准备回应、思考下一步或质疑对方论点的机制。这很难做到，因为我们的默认模式总是下一句对话。但我觉得如果你能像他说的那样，暂停下来，真正从整体上理解对方在说什么，效果会很显著。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was actually just reading that chapter and the next chapter is about this idea of the beginner's mind. I don't know if you remember that. I feel like people get sniped by Rick Rubin stuff. But anyway, I'm going to go down this thread. He talks about how AlphaZero or AlphaGo, the first AI thing that beat humans at Go and how there was this move it made, move 37 in the game that was just like ... The person the AI was playing walked out of the room. He's like, "I don't even know what just happened. This is out of anything I've ever imagined." And it won. And the lesson there it was trained not on what we've learned, but it trained itself and figured things out from first principles and then came up with this thing we've never even comprehended. And so it's a really good example of the power of coming from a beginner's mind and not being influenced by what's already been done.
turns.zh: 我刚好在读那一章，接下来讲的是初学者心态。你还记得吗？我感觉人们对里克·鲁宾的观点总是容易被误解。不过我要继续聊这个话题。他提到AlphaZero或AlphaGo，那个首次在围棋中击败人类的AI，它在比赛中第37步就做出一个令人震惊的举动，对手直接走出了房间。里克说：“我都不知道刚刚发生了什么。这完全超出了我的想象。”结果它赢了。这个案例说明，AI不是基于我们已有的知识训练，而是通过第一性原理自我学习，然后创造出我们难以理解的成果。这真是初学者心态的力量所在，不受既有思维的束缚。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Yeah. We have a walkthrough ritual that we do.
turns.zh: 对啊。我们也有一个走查流程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Tell me more.
turns.zh: 请多讲讲。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: The prompt is essentially put yourself in the shoes of someone who knows nothing about this topic whatsoever and have beginner's mind and then walk through with five or 10 people watching you and let's fix all the problems that we see.
turns.zh: 这个提示的核心是，让你设身处地地想像自己对这个话题一无所知，保持初学者的心态，然后在五到十个人观察你的情况下，逐步解决我们发现的问题。

turns.en: Okay. I want to talk about rituals. We're getting ahead of ourselves a little bit. Is there any other principles that you can share either just on a high level or in depth that you've come across? And I know people can go to your Substack and read this. And by the way, what's your Substack URL for people that want to check it out?
turns.zh: 好的。我想谈谈仪式感。我们可能有点跳题了。你有没有其他原则可以分享的，无论是高层面的还是深入的，你遇到过的？我知道人们可以去你的 Substack 阅读这些内容。顺便问一下，对于想查看的人，你的 Substack 网址是什么？

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Just lane.substack.com.
turns.zh: 就是 lane.substack.com。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sweet. We'll definitely link into it. Yeah. Any other principles?
turns.zh: 太好了。我们肯定会链接到那里的。是的。还有其他原则吗？

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: I think the other one is cathedrals, not bricks, and then the other one is proactive, not reactive. Cathedrals, not bricks I think is a classic one. I think I had a moment of realization and talking to Shishir in a one-on-one when I was at YouTube bemoaning the fact that my team wasn't performing to the potential that I thought they had. And he had a very pointed and unexpected question, which is like, "Do they know their cathedral? Do they have a cathedral?" And I'm sitting there like, "Man, what are you talking about? We're talking about performing as a team and you're asking me about cathedrals." And then he explained the cathedral story, which I can talk about. In that-
turns.zh: 我认为另一个是"大教堂，而非砖块"，另一个是"主动而非被动"。"大教堂，而非砖块"是一个经典的概念。我记得在 YouTube 的时候，我和 Shishir 单独交谈，抱怨我的团队表现没有达到我预期的水平。他提了一个非常尖锐且出乎意料的问题，问道："他们知道自己的大教堂吗？他们有大教堂吗？"我当时就想："天哪，你在说什么呢？我们在讨论团队表现问题，你却问我大教堂的事。" 然后他解释了大教堂的故事，我可以分享一下。在那个故事里——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's the cathedral story?
turns.zh: 大教堂的故事是什么？

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: It was quite clarifying.
turns.zh: 这个故事非常有启发性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Do share.
turns.zh: 是的。请分享一下。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Yeah. The cathedral story is basically you walk up to three people, they're laying bricks. You ask the first person, "What are you doing?" They say, "Well, I take the bricks from over here and I put them on that sack over there." You ask the second person, "What are you doing?" They say, "Well, I take this little cement and I put it on top of the brick that that person lays." You ask the third person, "What are you doing?" And they say, "Well, we're building a cathedral." And the core insight here is that you want your teams to feel like they're building a cathedral and not laying bricks. And I think it's really, really easy to do when PMs are really busy on a day-to-day to just be one task after the other, really execution oriented and maybe not take the time to help the team take a broader frame, open the aperture a little bit and have a view of what the cathedral is. And I think we've learned many times that one unexpected bit of this is that everybody needs to see a different facet of the cathedral. (00:26:22): So very often ... And I've made this mistake before plenty of times. Very often people will do a great writeup on vision or strategy or whatever it is and the result is people can't quite see their version of what this broader arc is or this broader cathedral is. And so one of the things that we have tried to do when we go through big planning cycles is show all the different sides of this. So instead of just having a writeup, we may have a writeup, we may couple that with a metric, we may couple that with directional mocks and what the billboard might look like or how our homepage may change. And really what we're trying to do is take the mystery out of the set of broader constraints or where we're headed. I think great product teams and great PM leaders tend to always orient their teams towards a broader cathedral as opposed to laying bricks.
turns.zh: 是的。关于大教堂的故事，大致是这样：你走过去看到三个人在砌砖。你问第一个人：“你在做什么？” 他们回答：“我从这边拿砖头，然后把它们放在那边的袋子里。” 你问第二个人：“你在做什么？” 他们回答：“我拿点水泥，涂在那个人砌好的砖头上。” 你问第三个人：“你在做什么？” 他们回答：“我们在建一座大教堂。” 这里的核心洞察是，你希望团队成员能感受到自己在建造大教堂，而不只是在砌砖。我认为，当产品经理们每天忙于琐事、只专注于执行而没有时间帮助团队拓宽视野、打开思路、了解大教堂全貌时，就很容易忽视这一点。我多次发现，一个意想不到的问题是，每个人都需要从不同角度看待大教堂。（00:26:22）所以很多时候……我自己也多次犯过这个错误。人们可能会写一份关于愿景或战略的精彩文档，但结果是大家无法清晰理解这幅更宏大的蓝图或大教堂的全貌。因此，在进行大型规划周期时，我们会尝试从多个角度展示问题。这时候我们不只是提供一份文档，还可能结合指标、方向性模型，以及广告牌可能的样子或主页的改进方案。实际上，我们的目标是消除更广泛约束条件或发展方向的神秘感。我认为优秀的产品团队和出色的产品经理往往会引导团队朝着更宏大的蓝图而努力，而不是局限于砌砖。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Such a beautiful metaphor. Reminds me of this other quote I just looked up while you're chatting. "If you want to build a ship, don't drum up the men to gather wood, divide the work and give orders. Instead teach them to yearn for the vast and endless sea."
turns.zh: 多么美妙的比喻啊。这让我想起你聊天时我刚查到的另一句名言：“如果你想造一艘船，不要召集人们去收集木材、分配工作和发号施令。相反，要教会他们渴望浩瀚无垠的大海。”

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Classic. Classic. It's Antoine.
turns.zh: 经典。经典。这是安托万·德·圣-埃克苏佩里说的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is right. Antoine de St. Exupery. Okay. Something I was curious about as you were chatting also is for folks that want to develop their own principles and define how they want to think about products, is there anything you found to be useful in helping emerge these into principles that you can come to? Is it just sitting around thinking? Is there anything else you've done that has helped you define these things?
turns.zh: 没错。安托万·德·圣-埃克苏佩里。对了。你聊天时我还好奇的是，对于那些想制定自己的原则、定义如何看待产品的人，有没有什么有用的方法能帮助他们形成这些原则？是靠冥想吗？还是做了其他什么有用的事？

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Probably two things. One is reading really broadly. So I think not just reading PM style literature. Like I said, I tend to get a lot of inspiration from outside of tech. I think that's one thing. I think the other thing is insofar as you get the opportunity to mentor other people, think about what you're saying to these people. Think about, okay, this person came to me with this challenge. What was my response? Why was that my response? Am I giving that response a lot of times? Okay, maybe this is a more deeply held belief. So I think noticing those instances was helpful for me.
turns.zh: 大概有两个方面。一是广泛阅读。我觉得不只是读产品经理相关的文献。就像我说的，我从科技领域以外获得了很多灵感。这是一方面。另一方面是，当你有机会指导他人时，要思考自己对他们的说法。比如，某个人来找你解决挑战时，你是怎么回应的？为什么那样回应？你是否经常给出同样的回应？好，也许这是一种更根深蒂固的信念。所以，我认为留意这些情况对我很有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are there any books or topics or areas that you found most inspirational when you talk about reading and studying other non-product tech?
turns.zh: 谈到阅读和研究非产品技术领域时，有没有哪些书籍、主题或领域能给您带来最大的启发？

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: I mean definitely sports. I would say sports is really interesting to me. Team sports. I've always been a huge fan of everything team sports. Storytelling. Go look at some of the best storytellers in the world and they're actually out there on a stage telling stories. There's a book called Storyworthy that I really like.
turns.zh: 我肯定会说体育。体育对我来说非常有趣，尤其是团队运动。我一直是团队运动的超级粉丝。讲故事方面，你可以看看世界上最出色的讲故事者，他们通常站在舞台上讲述故事。我特别喜欢一本叫《值得讲述的故事》的书。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was just going to mention that. That book is so good. Somebody mentioned this on the podcast and I read it. It's the most useful practical book for how to tell stories.
turns.zh: 我正想提到这本书。这本书太棒了。有人在播客上提到它，我读了之后发现，它是关于如何讲故事最实用的实用书籍。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: It's so good. The insight is amazing. Just in case your listeners are interested, the insight is basically the nugget of a great story is five seconds of transformation. So if you just orient everything else around that moment of transformation, then you end up usually telling a reasonably good story. I had a conversation with the author right after I read that book because I was just totally enamored with it. And then we ended up bringing him into Coda and he gave a great talk. So yeah, big plug for Matthew Dicks.
turns.zh: 真的很棒。里面的见解令人惊叹。以防听众感兴趣，关键点是，精彩故事的核心是五秒钟的转变时刻。所以如果你能围绕这个转变时刻来构建整个故事，通常就能讲出一个相当不错的故事。读完这本书后，我立即和作者进行了交流，因为我完全被它折服了。后来我们邀请他到Coda做了一场精彩的演讲。所以要大力推荐马修·迪克斯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other thing that stuck with me also from that same ... We're just going on all kinds of tangents. From that same insight is, and I watch movies completely differently now, where basically the characters you meet at the beginning of the story, they're going to be completely opposite at the end of the story because of this transformation that takes place. So I'm watching movies with my wife now, I'm like, "Okay, she's very shy right now. She's going to be very extroverted by the end of this movie." Or, "They love each other. Oh, they're going to have a lot of problems." That's so interesting. Oh, that's such a good idea. Okay, I'm going to get this guy on hopefully. And he's a Moth champion basically.
turns.zh: 同样来自这个见解的另一个让我印象深刻的点是，现在我看电影的方式完全不同了。基本上，在故事开始时遇到的角色，最终会因为发生的转变而截然不同。所以现在我和妻子一起看电影时，会想：“好吧，她现在很害羞，但电影结束时她会变得非常外向。”或者，“他们相爱了，但最终会有很多问题。”这太有趣了。哦，这真是个好主意。好吧，我希望能邀请到他。他基本上是Moth故事大赛的冠军。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Yeah. I would say as maybe a principal version of this, the way that you learn or the way that everyone including me learns new things is you go seek out the best at that given craft. So in this case, you go to the Moth StorySLAM you see some really good stories. If you ever watch these on YouTube. And then you just unpack what they're doing and how they're doing it. And then obviously I think the other way to learn quickly is to throw yourself in the deep end. So insofar as you can put yourself in situations that are uncomfortable or force you to do things like tell a story or force you to come up with a clear strategy, you should always opt into those, especially early in your career.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为学习的核心方法，或者说包括我在内的每个人学习新事物的核心方法，就是去寻找某个领域最优秀的人。就拿讲故事来说，你去参加Moth故事大赛，看一些非常精彩的故事。如果你有机会在YouTube上观看这些表演。然后你只需拆解他们是如何做到的，以及他们是如何操作的。显然，快速学习的另一种方法就是把自己置身于挑战之中。所以只要你能把自己置身于不舒适的环境中，或者迫使自己做一些事情，比如讲故事，或者制定清晰的策略，你就应该抓住这些机会，尤其是在职业生涯早期。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The first thing you said, that's basically the whole premise of this podcast. Find the best at all these things and learn from them, extract and share.
turns.zh: 你刚提到的第一点，这基本上就是这个播客的核心理念。找到这些领域的顶尖人物，向他们学习，提取并分享。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: And the world is much better for it. This podcast is an amazing resource.
turns.zh: 世界因此变得更美好。这个播客是一个了不起的资源。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thanks man.
turns.zh: 谢谢你，伙计。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: You've done something very special.
turns.zh: 你做了一件非常特别的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I appreciate it. This podcast episode is already very special. The point you just made reminds me of something that I heard you talk about, which is this oh shit moment. I don't know if it's related to what you shared of just giving people a sense of whether they're making progress in their career. Can you talk about that?
turns.zh: 非常感谢。这一期播客已经很特别了。你刚刚提到的观点让我想起之前听你讲过的“天啊”时刻。我不知道这是否与你分享的让人们了解自己职业生涯是否有进展的观点有关。你能谈谈这个吗？

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Sure. Yeah. I think I picked this up originally from Seth Godin, the author, and it just totally stuck with me. The basic thesis is that moments that stretch you or moments that you feel uncomfortable in or you find yourself saying, "Oh shit, I shouldn't be here," or, "I'm under qualified to be here," those are the moments you should be seeking out. Those are the moments that stretch you and give you a new foundation. And so I have found that they turn out to be a pretty good way to calibrate whether someone is growing in their career. So oftentimes you'll hear a career question like, "Hey, do you feel like you're growing in your role?" And that's a very ambiguous in my opinion way to ask this question. And a much sharper way is like, "Hey, how many, oh shit moments have you had in the last six months, year, two years, and what are they?" I think if you ask yourself that question and the answer is, "It's been a really long time since I've been stretched in some meaningful way or I've felt like I'm under qualified to be there," then it may be worth digging into.
turns.zh: 当然。是啊。我最初是从作家赛斯·高丁那里听到这个观点的，它一直让我印象深刻。基本观点是，当你面临挑战、感到不适，或者觉得“天啊，我不该在这里”或“我太不配待在这里”的时刻，这些正是你应该主动寻找的时刻。它们能拓展你的能力，为你奠定新的基础。所以我发现，这也是判断一个人职业生涯是否有进步的有效方法。人们常问：“你觉得自己在当前职位上成长了吗？”在我看来，这是一个模糊不清的问题。更尖锐的提问应该是：“过去六个月、一年、两年里，你经历过多少‘天啊’时刻？都是些什么情况？” 如果你问自己这个问题，答案是“很久没有真正面临挑战，或者觉得自己不配待在这里”，那么就值得深入探究了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is so good. Making me think about this podcast where I never wanted to do podcasts. I'm like I'm not a podcast person. I just want to sit there and type out newsletters. How cool is that? And I'm like, no, I got to do it because it's hard. And I'm glad I did it. It also reminds me of this quote that I love that I always think back to. "The cave you fear contains the treasure you seek."
turns.zh: 太棒了。这让我想起我从不愿做播客的经历。我当时觉得自己不适合做播客，只想坐着写新闻通讯。但我还是强迫自己去做了，因为这很困难。很高兴我这么做了。这也让我想起我一直珍视的一句话：“你害怕的洞穴，里面藏着你追寻的宝藏。”

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Nice. That reminds me of ... Have you read the book The Obstacle is the Way?
turns.zh: 不错。这让我想起……你读过《障碍即机遇》这本书吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No. Say More.
turns.zh: 没读过。多说几句。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: It's a great book by Ryan Holiday. And the core thesis is ... It's a bit about stoicism. But the core idea is essentially instead of running away from obstacles, you should be running toward them and that's where you experience either the most growth or the most profound moments of your life. He gives a lot of examples in that book of people throughout history who made that choice. And I think he's also given that talk to hundreds of sports teams. It's a good book. Worth reading.
turns.zh: 这是瑞安·霍利迪的一本好书。核心观点……书里讲了斯多葛主义。但核心思想是，不要逃避障碍，而要主动迎向它们。在那里，你要么获得最大的成长，要么经历人生最深刻的时刻。他书中举了很多历史人物的例子，说明他们如何做出这样的选择。我觉得他还给数百支运动队做过相关演讲。这本书很值得一读。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's so hard. It's so hard to do hard things, man. So we've been talking about principles of great product managers. You also spent a lot of time looking at the rituals of great product teams. And I know you're working on this handbook that I'm excited to learn more about. Can you just talk about ... I guess one, where this idea came from of studying rituals of great teams and also just how do you actually go about learning about these rituals? I know you have this really interesting process.
turns.zh: 这太难了。做难事真是太难了。我们一直在讨论优秀产品经理的原则，你也花了很多时间研究优秀产品团队的仪式。我知道你正在编写一本手册，我很期待了解更多。你能谈谈……首先，这个研究优秀团队仪式的想法从何而来？还有，你具体是如何去了解这些仪式的？我知道你有非常有趣的流程。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Yeah. In general, I'm a big believer in good design and good product starts with noticing. Tony Fadell has a great talk on this. So I think a bunch of us that are really obsessed with rituals, we just honestly try to be great at noticing. So see something happening with a customer, ask a few questions, get introduced to their team, hear about something interesting from a non-customer, ask for an intro, end up just probing and asking a lot of questions. And then in many cases nowadays with Coda, we're building new rituals alongside people. So someone has a creative idea about how to implement something and we're like partners or collaborators with them on that, which is honestly incredibly fun to just see people's creativity expressed in a tool and then by extension the social construct that they exist in. So that's a little bit about how we got started in that whole process. And then of course Shishir is writing a book called Rituals of Great Teams so we've been cataloging those. We've been hosting a bunch of rituals dinners where we basically get people together for a dinner and we usually have three or four presenters at those dinners. It's just a great chance to learn and think about how the engine runs in a lot of these companies.
turns.zh: 是的。总的来说，我非常重视好的设计，而好的产品始于观察。托尼·法德尔（Tony Fadell）对此有过精彩的演讲。所以我认为，我们中许多痴迷于仪式的人，都在努力成为善于观察的高手。比如，当我们注意到客户的某个需求时，会主动提问，认识他们的团队，从非客户那里听到有趣的想法后，会请求介绍，最终通过不断提问来深入了解。如今在Coda团队中，我们会与客户共同开发新仪式。当有人提出创新的实施方案时，我们会成为他们的合作伙伴，这种体验真的非常棒——既能见证人们在工具中展现创造力，又能延伸至他们所处的社交环境。这就是我们如何开启整个流程的初衷。当然，希希尔（Shishir）正在撰写《伟大团队的仪式》一书，我们一直在整理相关案例。同时，我们还举办了多场仪式晚宴，邀请三四位嘉宾分享见解，这为我们提供了绝佳的机会，深入了解许多公司的运作机制。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are some rituals that you've learned from these dinners and these and this research you've done that have really stuck with you?
turns.zh: 在这些晚宴和研究中，你学到了哪些令人印象深刻的仪式？

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: There are so many. It's hard to choose. Maybe I'll choose two that are top of mind. One is Dharmesh Shah has this ritual from HubSpot called flash tags. Have you heard of this?
turns.zh: 太多了，很难抉择。或许我会选两个最难忘的。第一个是达尔梅什·沙阿（Dharmesh Shah）在HubSpot推行的闪电标签（flash tags）仪式。你听说过吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 没有。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: We've all probably been in the situation where someone gives you feedback and you either under interpret it or over interpret it. And as an organization, I think the core principle here is like you want to be calibrated on how much to pay attention to a bit of feedback. And so he outlines four flash tags. He presented this in one of our dinners. And I absolutely love the phrasing of these as someone who's given a lot of feedback on product stuff in their career. So it ranges from ... I think it's FYI, suggestion, recommendation, plea. So FYI is basically like I had a thought, take it or leave it kind of thing. Suggestion is ... And he uses this hill dying metaphor. So is this a hill I'm going to die on? And FYI is there's no hill in sight. Suggestion is there's a hill. I'm not going to die on it but this is what I would do if I were you. You can take it or leave it. Recommendation is I'm climbing the hill. I'm not going to die here, but I've thought about this a lot, so don't ignore this. (00:37:41): And then the fourth one, plea, is hopefully rarely used in the organization. It's like, I don't like dying on hills. That's not what we do here. But this is a pretty good candidate for it. You should really trust me. And so we have ended up using that. I was actually just at an offsite and someone gave a lightning talk to our team on how valuable this has been just to calibrate, hey, we got 100 pieces of feedback and there's one plea. Okay, let's spend our time on that. Or there's a whole bunch of FYIs. I think we're fine. Let's keep going. No worries.
turns.zh: 我们都遇到过这样的情况：客户给出反馈后，我们要么误解其含义，要么反应过度。作为组织层面，我认为核心原则是，要根据反馈的重要性调整关注程度。他总结了四个闪电标签，并在我们的晚宴上做了讲解。作为在产品领域深有建树的人，我特别喜欢他对这些标签的描述。闪电标签涵盖四个层级：FYI（仅供参考）、建议、推荐和恳求。FYI相当于“我有个想法，爱听不听”；建议用“这是我要攀登的山峰”来比喻；推荐则是“我正在攀登这座山峰”；恳求则是“这座山峰值得攀登”。我们已经在实际工作中应用了这些标签。比如在一次公司活动上，某位同事给团队做了闪电演讲，强调反馈的重要性，尤其提到“我们收到100条反馈，其中只有一条是恳求。好吧，那就专注于它吧。”这样的案例非常实用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's amazing. It's interesting none of them are just do it this way. I imagine that's very intentional.
turns.zh: 太棒了。有趣的是，这些标签并非千篇一律。我想这背后一定有深意。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Yeah. Honestly it's a sign of ... In Dharmesh's case, I don't know him super well, but it's a sign of a really experienced leader to know that scale. But every time I look at the scale and I'm weighing where I am between suggestion or recommendation, I have to giggle to myself.
turns.zh: 是啊，说实话，这其实是……就拿达梅什（Dharmesh）来说吧，我和他不太熟，但他能清楚认识到这种规模差异，这恰恰说明他是个经验丰富的领导者。不过每次我看到这些反馈意见，在决定是给出建议还是推荐时，我都会忍不住暗自发笑。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And how do you actually use it? In the feedback you put a hashtag plea kind of thing?
turns.zh: 那具体怎么用呢？你是在反馈中加上标签之类的吗？

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: The way gets used in code docs and the way I think other companies have made it a ritual is you'll have a feedback table and you'll write your feedback and then there'll just be a little select list and you can select between those four. And usually what people do is they include the description so you can as you're choosing it, think do I really feel that strongly about this? And honestly, it's good hygiene. Otherwise, every bit of feedback is taken the same. Which just fundamentally the impact of that is it slows everything down because now you're looking at a list of 100 pieces of feedback and you're going like, "Oh man, we got to address all this feedback." Whereas as soon as you distinguish between what's most important, it's much easier to sort through that.
turns.zh: 这种方法常用于代码文档，我觉得其他公司也把它当作一种惯例。通常会有一个反馈表格，你写下自己的反馈，然后会出现一个小选项列表，你可以在四个选项中选择。人们通常会附上详细描述，这样在选择时就能思考：我对这件事的看法真的有那么强烈吗？说实话，这是一种良好的沟通规范。否则，每条反馈都会被同等对待。这样做的最终影响就是拖慢了整个进程，因为你要面对100条反馈，然后不得不说："天哪，我们得处理所有这些反馈。"而一旦你区分了最重要的反馈，整理起来就会容易得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What about if it's in person? Do you say this is a plea or this is a FYI?
turns.zh: 那如果是面对面交流呢？你会说这是请求还是仅供参考？

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Oh, I've definitely heard that in many meetings. Are you making a recommendation or are you making a plea?
turns.zh: 哦，我在很多会议上都听到过这种说法。你是在提出建议还是请求帮助？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: And making the person think through that choice I think is just a very helpful shared language.
turns.zh: 让对方思考自己的选择，我觉得这是一种非常有用的沟通方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine one of the other benefits of this is I think most leaders that rise up the ranks eventually realize anything they say in a meeting is going to be taken really seriously and the team's going to rush back and be like, "Oh, Lane told us to change this thing." I imagine it helps you just make it clear. No, you don't need to actually change this. It's just my thoughts.
turns.zh: 我觉得这样做还有一个好处，那就是大多数晋升的领导者最终都会意识到，他们在会议上说的任何话都会被认真对待，团队成员会赶紧跑回去说："哦，莱恩让我们改这个。"我觉得这能让你明确表达：不，你不需要真的改这个。这只是我的想法。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Yeah. Exactly. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊，就是这样。是啊。
