turns.zh: 太棒了。本期节目由领先的全身癌症筛查公司Ezra赞助。实际上，我今年早些时候曾使用过Ezra的服务——与本播客无关，完全自费体验。因为我妻子做过筛查并很满意，而随着年龄增长，我也特别想了解身体是否有需要关注的问题。筛查流程是这样：预约后，穿上他们提供的精美丝质睡衣（用后可保留），进入MRI扫描仪接受30至45分钟的检查。一周后，会收到详细报告，里面会指出身体存在的隐患。幸运的是，我的筛查结果“无异常”，即未发现癌症，但背部有问题，下个月我会去医院进一步检查，可能是因为长时间伏案工作所致。据美国癌症协会数据，半数男性和三分之一女性一生中都会患上癌症，其中半数确诊时已是晚期。Ezra团队已帮助13%的客户早期发现癌症，50%客户发现动脉瘤、椎间盘突出等临床重要问题。Ezra通过AI驱动的全身MRI技术，可筛查13个器官的500种疾病，最近推出了全球首款30分钟全身扫描服务，价格也最为亲民。扫描过程无创无辐射。Ezra为听众提供首扫150美元优惠，优惠码：Lenny150。可登录ezra.com/lenny或E-Z-R-A.com/lenny预约扫描。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: I guess one that I get asked about a lot on our team is called Catalyst. And I guess maybe to set some context on this one, in most product teams, the review forum is just a really important part of the product development process. And the core insight for most review forums or product reviews or decision forums is that they generally suffer from two problems that are hard to spot unless you've sat through hundreds of them. The first is they have standing attendees, and the second is they're normally single-threaded, meaning they're normally one topic at a time. So maybe I'll talk about both of those because I think they're not exactly intuitive. So when you think about what happens with a standing set of attendees, you either have the situation where you have too many people in the meeting or you have not enough people in the meeting, and both of those can cause problems. (00:43:25): So if you've ever been in a meeting, I certainly have, where it's like, "Hey, do we have the salesperson who knows most about this or do we have the engineer who's actually implementing this here? Oh, great. They're not here? They're not a part of the standing set of attendees?" You either have to reschedule the meeting or worse, you just do the discussion without the person who's most knowledgeable, which seems crazy in retrospect. The second problem is single-threaded. So one topic at a time. So if you think about if a product development process is somewhat of a chaotic assembly line for a second, your review or your decision forum ends up being a big time bottleneck in many cases. And obviously you want to be in a situation where product people have a lot of autonomy and they can make most of the decisions themselves. And I'm a big believer in decentralized leadership and all of that, but there are things that cut across the company that need to get reviewed by a broader set of stakeholders. (00:44:29): And so what happens when those things are single threaded is either the meeting is really long, so it's a three-hour review meeting once a week, and by the end everyone is about to fall asleep, or it's really short and it's really hard to get on the calendar. You're like, "Oh, can we get on the calendar in two weeks?" And the downside of the not being able to get on the calendar is that now you've just slowed down the whole velocity of the company because the throughput of your review meeting is really slow. So we built Catalyst to really solve those two problems. And so the way it works is it's essentially three one hour blocks throughout the week, and the assumption is that the whole company is free. So you can get anyone in the company for those three hours. And each topic has essentially four roles. Driver, maker, braintrust, and interested. It's a very transparent system. (00:45:28): So a salesperson can say, "Oh, I'm interested in this product development review. I'm just going to mark myself as interested." And then the driver is the person who's actually going to drive the meeting, drive the decision, drive the outcome, things like that. And basically, this is all centralized in one doc. And what happens is the day before, that hold that's on calendar gets removed, and then you have specific topics that get added. So there may be three topics going all at the same time because they don't have overlapping attendees. And the impact of this, I think if you really watch it in progress is huge. You basically have many topics running all at the same time, so the throughput is much better and you have the right attendees every single time, and you have a clear set of drivers and roles in these meetings. So that means that we can review work much, much faster with the right people, and ideally that results in more value to our customers, more things getting shipped, just a higher velocity organization. So that's one that we get asked about a lot. And actually a couple of weeks ago, we spent a while remaking the template for that one.
turns.zh:
想必在我们团队里，被问得最多的一个工具叫做Catalyst。先来解释一下背景吧：在大多数产品团队中，评审论坛都是产品开发流程中至关重要的一环。但大多数评审论坛、产品评审或决策论坛都存在两个难以察觉的问题，除非你亲身经历过数百次会议。第一个问题是固定参会人员机制，第二个问题是单线程讨论模式，即每次只讨论一个议题。接下来我会详细解析这两个问题，因为它们确实不符合直观认知。

（00:43:25）：说到固定参会人员机制，会议要么人太多，要么人太少。这两种情况都会引发问题。比如在会议上，你可能会遇到这样的情况：“销售人员最了解这个产品，工程师又实际负责实施？哦，他们不在？他们不是固定参会人员？”要么重新安排会议，要么只能在没有最有经验的人的情况下讨论问题，事后看来这种做法简直荒谬。

第二个问题是单线程讨论模式，即每次只讨论一个议题。假设产品开发流程是一个混乱的流水线，那么评审或决策论坛往往成为整个过程中的瓶颈。显然，我们希望产品团队拥有高度自主权，能自主做出大部分决策。我非常支持去中心化领导力等理念，但有些跨部门的问题确实需要更广泛的利益相关者参与评审。

（00:44:29）：当这些问题陷入单线程讨论模式时，会议要么时间过长，比如每周三小时的评审，结束时所有人都昏昏欲睡；要么排期太难，拖到两周后才行。排期延迟会拖慢整个公司的节奏，因为评审会议的效率太低。因此我们开发了Catalyst来解决这两个问题。其核心机制是每周三次一小时的会议，假设全公司资源可用，所以三小时内能召集所有人。每个议题设有四个角色：驱动者、执行者、智囊团和感兴趣者。整个系统高度透明。

（00:45:28）：比如销售人员可以标注“对此次评审感兴趣”，驱动者负责推动会议进程、做出决策、达成结果等。这一切都集中在一个文档中。具体流程是前一天解除原有会议预约，添加新议题。多个议题可同时进行，因为参会人员不重叠。实际效果显著：多个议题并行推进，效率大增，每次都能召集到合适的参会人员。
在这些会议中，要明确各方的职责和角色。这意味着，我们能与合适的人员更高效地审阅工作成果，最终为客户创造更多价值，推动更多项目落地，让整个组织的运作效率显著提升。这是我们经常被问到的问题。实际上，几周前，我们花了不少时间重新设计了相关模板。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that ritual. You actually wrote even in more depth in the post that we worked together on how Coda builds product, which we'll link to if folks want to try this out and you link to actual templates people can actually use it their companies. When someone's listening to this and they're like, "Oh, wow, this is extremely cool," how easy is it do you find for people to take a ritual from a company and implement it? How much is cultural and it's hard to transplant, or do you find people can take this Catalyst idea plug and play at a lot of companies?
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这种仪式感。你在我们合作的帖子中更深入地阐述了Coda如何进行产品开发，如果大家想尝试的话，我们会附上链接。还有你提到的实际模板，人们可以直接在自己的公司使用。当有人听完后感叹“哇，太酷了”，你觉得让人们从其他公司借鉴并实施这种仪式有多容易？这其中有多少是文化差异导致难以移植的，还是说很多公司都能直接套用Catalyst的思路？

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Yeah. I think it depends a lot on what your role in the company is. Maybe to say the extremes for a second, if you're a brand new PM to an organization, you probably shouldn't go try to remake the whole product review cycle that the head of product is really passionate about and has crafted. But you can probably take a decision template or some interesting ritual that has facilitated a team in the past and use it with your team. Another one of my favorites there is a hundred dollar voting. We use that a lot in the context of planning, and I find that creative rituals like that are easy to pick up for teams because oftentimes it's like, okay ... And maybe I'll describe the ritual real quick.
turns.zh: 是的。我觉得这很大程度上取决于你在公司中的角色。说极端一点，如果你是一个新加入的PM，试图重构产品负责人非常热衷且精心设计的整个产品评审周期，可能不太明智。但你或许可以借鉴过去团队成功运用的决策模板或创新仪式。比如“百元投票”（hundred dollar voting），我们在规划过程中经常使用。我发现这类创意仪式对团队易于接受，因为通常大家会想：“好吧……”。或许我可以快速描述一下这个仪式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I was going to ask.
turns.zh: 好的，我正想问呢。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: The ritual is essentially you can take any set of problems or solutions or themes or whatever you want to get people's input on, and you put those into a table and then people can basically vote with their dollars and usually you allocate $100. And so people will go through and say, "Oh, I want to allocate $10 to this and $20 to this and $50 to this because I think it's really important." And I have found that especially in planning processes, little rituals like this are great at getting the elephant in the room out. So it's like, "Oh wow, we have a huge spread on this one particular problem. You think it's a huge problem. I don't think it's a problem at all. Let's talk about it." Going back to the thesis of turning ambiguity into clarity, a lot of this is like we're trying to get the ambiguous stuff out there so that we can make it more clear. (00:49:03): And so I use that as an example because you can be a brand new PM, run a brainstorm, run a planning session like that, and you're probably going to get great feedback. People are probably going to go, "This is cool. I've never done this before." Now to go to the other side of the spectrum, we help a lot of companies that want to remake a whole process. They want to remake a review system like Catalyst or they want to remake their decision rituals. And so in that sense, we're usually talking to a head of product or director of product or VP of product and someone who tends to have a lot more agency over the way that the team works.
turns.zh: 这种仪式本质上是，你可以选取任何一组需要收集意见的问题、解决方案或主题，然后把它们列入表格，人们可以用“美元投票”进行决策，通常每人分配100美元。人们会逐一投票，比如：“我愿意为这个问题分配10美元，为那个问题分配20美元，为这个问题分配50美元，因为我认为它很重要。” 我发现这种仪式特别适用于规划过程，能把潜藏的矛盾暴露出来。比如：“哇，我们对这个问题的看法分歧很大。你觉得这是个大问题，而我根本不认为这是个问题。我们来讨论一下吧。” 回归到将模糊性转化为清晰性的核心理念，关键在于把模糊的问题暴露出来，让大家更清楚状况。（00:49:03）：所以我以这个为例，因为你可以作为新入职的PM，组织头脑风暴或规划会议，通常能获得很好的反馈。人们可能会说：“这太酷了，我从没这么做过。” 再说另一个极端，我们帮助很多公司彻底重建整个流程。他们想重建Catalyst这样的评审系统，或者重建决策仪式。在这种情况下，我们通常与产品负责人、产品总监或产品副总裁合作，这些人对团队的工作方式有更大的决策权。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Coda is interesting in that it feels like you have pretty stable processes for planning and reviews. I find most companies just every six months rethink a lot of these things. I guess that's probably a sign that you found something that's really good and works and you don't have to redo it. How much are you radically changing the way you operate versus working in similar ways? How do you think about that percentage wise?
turns.zh: Coda的有趣之处在于，它似乎有相当稳定的规划和评审流程。我发现大多数公司每六个月就会重新审视这些流程。这或许说明你们找到了真正有效的方案，无需反复改进。相较于彻底变革，你们在多大程度上保持了原有模式？从比例上看，你们是如何考虑的？

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: People are always coming up with new creative ways to make their teams run better, make decisions go smoother. And we're continuously adopting those, but there's definitely a backbone of the system. The backbone of the system is Catalyst and tag-ups and the concept called Bullpen. And then there'll be a lot of iteration on top of that. And even those systems went through a lot of iteration. I talked about how the calendar hold got removed and then individual topics got added. That took us launching automations and the ability to add things to calendar in order for that whole process to really work. So in the years prior to us launching that, we did it very manually. So I think there's still a lot of creativity that I see every day. (00:51:06): So I'll give one quick example. One of our PM leads on core product, this guy Nathan, he basically saw that a lot of decisions had a lot of different stakeholders because he's in the core product. And now he's leading the core product team so he's trying to figure out what guidance do I give to each of these PMs on who to involve in these decisions? Because every one of these with core product feels like they impact everybody. And so a very simple thing that he did probably in the last six months was he had a table of all the upcoming decisions and then at a tag-up ... Which I can explain if you want. But basically with a small set of stakeholders, he had all the upcoming decisions and then he let people hit a little reaction and say, "Oh, I don't need to be involved. Just notify me of the decision after." Or, "Hey, I have some opinions, but you can keep going." Or, "No, I really want to be heavily involved in this decision." (00:52:10): And it was such a pro move. It was such a, I've been through a million of these. I don't want to treat every one of them the same because if I do, it's going to slow down the velocity of this whole organization. And so instead, the majority of those, Shishir or I or Oliver, the head of engineering will say, "I may have some opinions, but keep going." That's often the default. And then there are plenty where we say, "Just notify us of the decision after." And in doing that, Nathan can now give better guidance to the PMs on his team and say, "Hey, you don't really need to involve as wide a group as you think, so just keep going and check in later." So I think those types of little iterations are usually based on a really good insight.
turns.zh:
人们总是在想出新的创新方法，让团队运作更高效，决策更顺畅。我们一直在采纳这些方法，但系统的核心架构始终不变。系统的核心架构包括Catalyst、Tag-ups以及名为Bullpen的理念。除此之外，系统还需要不断迭代。就连这些系统也经历了多次迭代。我曾提到过日历持有功能被移除，随后又添加了单独的主题。这就需要我们推出自动化功能，并能在日历中添加内容，才能让整个流程真正高效运转。在推出这些功能之前的几年里，我们都是手动操作的。所以我认为每天都能看到很多创新之处。

（00:51:06）：我举个快速例子。我们的核心产品PM负责人Nathan发现，由于他身处核心产品团队，许多决策都涉及多个利益相关方。现在他领导着核心产品团队，试图为每个PM提供指导，告诉他们在这些决策中该邀请谁参与？因为核心产品团队的每个决策都感觉会影响到所有人。过去六个月里，他做了一件很简单的事：制作一张即将做出的决策清单，然后在Tag-ups会议上……如果您想了解具体过程，我可以解释。但基本上，他会让一小部分利益相关方参与其中，列出所有即将做出的决策。参与者可以点击反应按钮，选择“我不需要参与，直接通知我决策结果即可”、“我有一些意见，但你可以继续推进”或“不，我真的想深度参与这个决策”。

（00:52:10）：这真是高明之举。我经历过无数类似情况。我不想对每个决策都一视同仁，因为那样会拖慢整个组织的运转速度。因此，大多数情况下，Shishir、我或工程部主管Oliver会说：“我可能有一些意见，但继续推进吧。”这通常是默认回应。当然，也有许多情况下，我们会说：“直接通知我们决策结果即可。”通过这些举措，Nathan现在能为团队中的PM们提供更好的指导，告诉他们：“其实不需要让那么多人参与，继续推进后续再沟通。”所以我认为这些小小的迭代通常基于深刻的洞察。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It sounds like a dream come true for a platform team to reduce how many people have to be involved in all your planning and decision making. And that process in which you call it tag-up, maybe just briefly explain it and then I want to talk about this handbook you're working on, which is going to I think, cover a lot of these things.
turns.zh: 对于一个平台团队来说，减少参与规划和决策的人数听起来像是美梦成真。而你们称之为Tag-ups的流程，能否简要解释一下？然后我想谈谈你们正在编写的手册，我认为它会涵盖很多这方面的内容。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Tag-up is based on this insight that a lot of work and project work tends to get discussed in one-on-ones. And actually it's really an anti-pattern. It's a pattern you should try to avoid. So if you're talking to your manager about product work, what's not happening in that moment is your eng lead and your design lead, they're not hearing that. And so you end up with this big game of telephone where you'll have a conversation with your manager in a one-on-one, they'll go back and translate to their engineering and design lead, and of course the fidelity of the game of telephone, something is lost in all of those transmissions. And so the core idea is have a group one-on-one with the key stakeholders. And so we have this concept of braintrust that's modeled off after Pixar's braintrust. (00:54:11): And so we'll have a tag-up with a small set of people from a given team, or sometimes we have larger groups, and then they meet with their braintrust and it's once a week. It's the same mindset of a one-on-one. It's their time. So anything that they need to unblock a decision or to make progress, they should use that time for. And they often start by reviewing OKRs and metrics and things like that. But then we generally get into a table of topics. Anyone can add a topic. Those topics are up voted, so people will react and then the table will sort itself. And then we'll say, "Okay, this is clearly the topic on people's mind." And that's a version of what we call Dory, which I can talk about. But essentially the principle is you should discuss that project work with the whole group there. With the whole triad there. And oftentimes with the sales person there and with the marketer there and with everybody else. So I found that that is just a really good practice to try to move a lot of that work out of one-on-ones and into a small group setting.
turns.zh: 标签会议（Tag-up）的核心理念源于这样一个观察：许多工作和项目讨论往往是在一对一的会议中进行的。但这其实是一种反模式，是我们应当避免的做法。举个例子，如果你和经理讨论产品工作，此刻工程主管和设计主管并未参与讨论。于是整个过程就如同玩"传话游戏"——你和经理一对一沟通后，他们再将信息传达给工程和设计团队，信息在层层传递中难免出现偏差。因此，关键在于与核心利益相关者进行集体一对一会议。我们借鉴皮克斯的"智囊团"模式，定期组织小型团队的标签会议（每周一次），共同探讨项目进展。会议遵循一对一的核心理念——这是属于团队成员的专属时间。无论是破解决策障碍还是推进项目进展，都应充分利用这段专属时间。会议通常从复盘OKR与关键指标开始，随后进入主题讨论环节。任何人都可以提出议题，议题会通过投票机制筛选，最终汇总出团队关注的核心议题。这套机制被我们称为"多莉法则"（Dory），我稍后会详细介绍。但核心原则是，所有项目讨论都应在完整的三角团队（工程、设计、产品）参与下进行，必要时可邀请销售和市场人员等多方参与。我发现这种模式能有效将一对一会议中的大量工作转移至集体讨论平台。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. So you're working on a handbook that's collecting a lot of these rituals. Talk about that and then when can people maybe look for it?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，那你正在编写的手册里汇集了很多这样的实践流程。能讲讲这个手册的情况吗？什么时候能让大家看到？

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: One of the realizations I had the other day, probably a month or two ago when we started working on this thing, was I was talking to someone about Catalyst and a couple other concepts, and they were like, "I get it. I'm sold. I want to implement some of these things. Where do I look?" And so I found myself sending them a bunch of links to individual templates. So that cued us into the fact that we needed to have a better core handbook for teams that wanted to adopt some of these rituals and also learn from all the rituals that we have learned from and feel very fortunate to have partnered with so many customers on. And so what we did was started writing this handbook, and it's going to come out hopefully by the time this recording is done. And in it, we'll talk about everything from rituals like Catalyst to decision rituals to a lot of planning and strategy and roadmaps, that kind of stuff. And trying to pull out the most interesting patterns and also give people a pretty practical view of how to implement these things. I think that's what has been lacking sometimes.
turns.zh: 最近我意识到一个问题，大概是在一两个月前我们开始做这件事的时候。当时我和某个人聊到Catalyst和其他一些概念，他们说："我懂了，被说服了。我想实施其中一些东西。去哪里找资源呢？"于是我发现自己只能给他们发一堆单独模板的链接。这让我们意识到，确实需要为想采用这些实践的团队准备一份更完善的核心手册，同时总结我们从客户身上学到的成功经验。于是我们着手编写这份手册，希望能在本次录制结束前发布。手册将涵盖从Catalyst这样的流程，到决策机制，再到规划、战略和路线图等多个方面。我们会提取最有趣的实践模式，并为大家提供切实可行的实施指南。我觉得这正是当前实践中常常缺失的部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. We'll definitely link to that. Hopefully it's live by the time goes out. We'll make it happen. I know also you said Shishir's working on a book that's related and basically rituals of great teams and Shishir was on the podcast and he talked about Dory, so we don't have to get into that. If people want to learn about Dory, they can watch that episode. It was one of the earliest episodes actually. One of the most popular.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们肯定会把这篇文章链接起来的。希望它能在节目播出前上线。我们会确保做到的。我还知道你提到希希尔正在写一本相关书籍，主要讲伟大团队的仪式流程。希希尔上次参加播客时提到了多莉（Dory），我们就不必再多说了。如果有人想了解多莉，可以去看那期节目。事实上那是我们最早的节目之一，也是最受欢迎的节目之一。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Yeah. I remember that.
turns.zh: 是的，我记得。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Cool. I have a bunch of random questions now. I'm just going to go in a few different directions. One is, you wrote this post that you call Learn by Making, Not Talking. Is that another principle by the way? Is that amongst your many principles?
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。我现在有几个随机的问题。我想从几个不同的方向入手。第一个问题是，你写了一篇名为《以实践而非空谈来学习》的文章。这是你的另一条原则吗？是你的众多原则之一吗？

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Awesome. So in that post, which we'll link to, you share this story of how you and the YouTube team came up with skippable ads, which I didn't realize it was such a controversial ... But in thinking about it, obviously letting people skip ads, I could see why people were not excited about that. Could you just tell that story? And basically it's like the story of how skippable ads on YouTube came about?
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。在那篇文章里（我们会链接的），你分享了你和YouTube团队如何开发跳过广告功能的故事。我之前没意识到这曾引发那么大的争议……但仔细想想，让用户跳过广告，我能理解为什么人们对此不感兴趣。你能讲讲这个故事吗？基本上就是YouTube跳过广告功能的诞生过程吗？

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Yeah. So I moved over to YouTube shortly after the acquisition. It was an amazing tight-knit team. It definitely felt like the Wild West. We were getting sued by Viacom for a billion dollars when that was a lot of money. No advertiser wanted to talk to us. It was essentially viewed as a site of cat videos and dogs on skateboards and things like that. And then I guess the other context, the sales team was very nascent and all they wanted to sell was the homepage and for good reason. That was where you made your money as a salesperson. And so I had just been sponsored by Salar and Shishir to become a PM. It's a longer story that I'll leave out for now and we can go into. But on day one of being a PM, Shishir's like, "Great. You're the new guy. You get the project that nobody else wants and that's called skippable ads. And we've got this crazy idea that we can align the incentives of advertisers and viewers and creatives in this really clever way by putting a skip button on the ad and then charging people per views." And the latter part we hadn't quite cemented yet, but it was part of the core idea. (00:59:04): And so the thing I write about in this post is as a new PM, this feels like a really consequential decision. It's like we've got this new product idea. Nobody really wants it. Advertisers don't want it. The sales team doesn't want it. And it's a very unproven thesis. And so the thing I write about is these are the types of things that you can debate for months or years. And I was sitting in a one-on-one with this guy named Phil Farhi who's an amazing product leader and was my boss at the time. And we're trying to figure out what to do and how to handle all the different dynamics. And he just stops and he's like, "You know what? Just test the extremes. Start the experiment tomorrow. We'll figure it out." Essentially. (00:59:49): And I think his point was like, look, we can debate this forever. So I would rather us see the upper and lower bounds of how good this could be or how bad this is going to be immediately. And so we launched a set of experiments. This guy Jamie Kerns who's still there. Tiny little skip button on one experiment, giant skip button that covered the entire player on the other side of the experiment. And within a few weeks, I think we had developed some conviction based on some very directional data that we were onto something. And so the lesson that I took, this is many years ago and I've seen this proven out hundreds of times since, is stop talking about it and go make something. Go run an experiment. Go make a prototype, go write a doc, go make a mock. Just don't talk about it. (01:00:49): And I found that also as a leader, people really follow that concept. And I also found that it transcends level. I am not talking just to ICPMs. I'm talking to heads of product and CPOs and CEOs to some degree. You should always be out there trying to learn by expressing your ideas and putting them out there. And that's much more valuable in many cases than pontificating about it or having endless circular discussions on it.
turns.zh: 是的。收购完成后不久，我就转到了YouTube。当时那是一个非常紧密团结的团队。整个氛围就像狂野西部。当时维亚康姆（Viacom）起诉我们索赔十亿美元——那可是一大笔钱——而且没有广告商愿意和我们合作。人们普遍认为YouTube就是个放猫视频、狗狗玩滑板之类内容的网站。再说销售团队当时还很不成熟，他们只想卖首页广告——这确实是个赚钱的好方法。后来Salar和Shishir资助我成为产品经理。这是个很长的故事，暂且不表。但我刚上任产品经理的第一天，Shishir就对我说：“不错，你是新来的。接手一个没人要的项目——可跳过广告。我们的核心理念是，通过在广告上加跳过按钮，再按次数收费，让广告商、观众和创作者的利益达成完美平衡。”后半部分我们当时还没完全确定，但这是核心思路的一部分。（00:59:04）：我在这篇文章里写道，作为新任产品经理，面对这个新产品理念时，感觉这是一个非常重要的决策。没人看好它，广告商不买账，销售团队也反对，而且这还是个未经证实的理论。所以我写到，这些都是可以争论数月甚至数年的问题。当时我和产品负责人Phil Farhi单独谈话，他是个很棒的产品领袖，也是我当时的上司。我们试图理清各种复杂因素。他突然停下来说：“知道吗？直接测试极端方案。明天就开始实验。边做边调整。”大致就是这个意思。（00:59:49）：他的意思是，讨论太久没意义，不如马上验证上限和下限。于是我们启动了一系列实验。其中一个实验是微小的跳过按钮，另一个实验则用巨大的按钮覆盖整个播放器。几周后，基于有指导性的数据，我们确信这个方向是对的。从中得到的教训是——这是多年前的事了，此后又验证了无数次——别光说不做，直接行动。做实验、写原型、写文档、做模型，别空谈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It makes me think a little bit about Twitter where they spent years just thinking about the edit button or all these different changes. They're so scared, they did so much research and then now they're changing things left and right. Everything's fine. Everyone's still using it. It shows you that you don't have to be so delicate.
turns.zh: 这让我想起Twitter，他们花了好几年讨论编辑按钮和各种改动。太谨小慎微了，做了太多调研，现在又到处改动。一切安好，用户还在用。可见没必要太在意细节。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Yes. It's almost never as bad as you think it's going to be. So yeah, it's just a question of how much better it can be oftentimes.
turns.zh: 是的。情况往往比你想象的要好得多。所以说，有时候关键在于它还能好到什么程度。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned in your early career ... We talked about your Alaska guide phase. Something else I saw is that you were on the AdWords approval team. You basically were reviewing ads people submitted to run on AdWords and that's how you started in tech. So I guess first of all, is that true? And then second of all, how did you graduate from that phase and become this Chief Product Officer of one of the fastest growing, most interesting companies in the world?
turns.zh: 你提到了自己职业生涯早期……我们之前聊过你在阿拉斯加做导游的阶段。我还了解到你曾在AdWords审核团队工作，当时你主要负责审核用户提交的AdWords广告，这就是你涉足科技行业的起点。首先，我想确认一下这是否属实？其次，你是如何从那个阶段过渡到如今成为全球增长最快、最具创新力的公司之一的首席产品官的呢？

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: That was a really memorable time. There's an amazing cohort of people that started in tech. I think there was 200 or 300 of us at that time and then eventually thousands that started in Sheryl Sandberg's organization. I guess maybe some quick context. Before running ads on google.com at that time, you had to have them manually approved by a human before that was handled by machine learning and outsourced to other countries. And so there was this process where basically an ad would show up on your screen, you would mark it family safe, non-family safe, porn. And then based on that, it would either run or it wouldn't. And actually, funny enough, some of my most successful friends were terrible at the approval event. They failed the rote task of approving ads. They just couldn't handle it and they went on to be really, really successful. (01:03:08): So after working on ad approvals, at that time, I moved to chat support. It was basically when AdWords was launching chat support. I remember very fondly having two chats, chatting with two advertisers at once. Moved on to phone support. That was eight hours a day of talking to AdWords customers. Really a total rollercoaster ride. It was basically one minute you would pick up the phone and it would be someone from a Fortune 100 company trying to spend millions of dollars on AdWords and then the next minute you would be on the phone with a psychic or a taxi driver that was warring with their compatriots over some really specific keyword. I think there were two lessons that I would draw from this. One is I had a mentor at the time and his advice when I was starting my career was basically you have to get customer facing from the very beginning because you're going to end up serving a customer your whole career. Even when you're the CEO of a company, you're going to be serving a customer. So you better get really good at being in any customer scenario and being able to handle it. And so I think that that turned out to be insanely good advice. And if I think about a piece of advice that I give out to people who are early in their career, I've definitely recycled that advice. (01:04:29): I think the other thing that I took away from that experience was it's just a great lesson in when people don't actually care about your product. So in AdWord's case, people did not care about AdWords. You were the expert on it and you're trying to tell them about ad groups and how this ad format works and blah, blah. And most of the time people are like, "Dude, I'm a small business owner. I'm trying to get people to come to my auto mechanic store." Or, "I'm trying to get people to come to my taxi service," or whatever it was. I don't care. Basically the product had to get out of the way and really just drive impact for the customer. It was like they just want more phone calls or they want more people in the store. So those are I think two pieces that I think about from those days still. (01:05:21): And then I worked in a variety of other roles. I worked in a role called product specialist, which is an awesome role back when there were 15 product specialists at Google. For me, that was an amazing time because I was getting to sit on seven or eight different core product teams. And in my observation, these days, most PMs don't get to sit on other people's core teams. And so I had these three or four years of just ... I call it a masterclass in PMing because I was getting to watch what was working for some PMs and what wasn't working for other PMs and just taking notes behind the scenes. So that was a really influential role. And then went on to various PM roles at Google and YouTube.
turns.zh:
那真是一段难忘的时光。当时有一群了不起的人加入了科技行业。我记得当时我们大概有200到300人，后来谢丽尔·桑德伯格的团队又吸纳了数千名新成员。先说点背景吧。在谷歌广告平台投放广告时，广告内容必须经过人工审核才能上线，后面才逐渐引入机器学习技术并将审核外包给其他国家。当时的审核流程是这样的，用户看到广告后需要标注其是否适合家庭观看、是否不宜观看、是否包含色情内容。根据这些标注，广告要么被批准，要么被拒绝。说个有趣的事，我一些最成功的朋友在审核环节表现得很糟糕。他们连最基本的审核任务都完成不了，但最终还是取得了巨大成功。

（01:03:08）：在负责广告审核工作后，我转到了聊天支持部门。当时AdWords刚推出聊天支持功能。我记得最难忘的经历是同时和两个广告主聊天，帮助他们解决问题。后来又转到电话支持部门，每天要接听八小时的AdWords用户来电。那种体验真是过山车般的刺激。前一分钟接到《财富》100强公司的电话，他们想花数百万美元投放广告；下一分钟又和某位灵媒或出租车司机争论某个关键词的排名问题。我从中总结了两点经验：一是导师曾告诉我，职业生涯初期必须亲自面对客户，因为你终身都要为客户服务——即便身为CEO，也要为用户创造价值。二是用户根本不在乎你的产品。在AdWords案例中，用户根本不关心产品本身。你讲解广告组、广告格式时，他们往往说：“老兄，我是小企业主，只想推广汽车修理店。”或者“我要推广出租车服务”等等。你得让产品退居二线，专注于为客户创造价值。

（01:04:29）：还有一点启发是，当用户不在乎产品时，该如何应对。以AdWords为例，用户根本不关注技术细节。你要教他们广告组如何设置、广告格式如何优化，但他们只关心转化效果。比如“我要更多电话咨询”或“吸引更多店铺访客”。这让我意识到，产品必须让用户受益，满足他们的核心需求。

（01:05:21）：后来我还担任过其他角色，比如产品专员。在谷歌早期，这个职位很棒，当时有15位产品专员。我能参与七八个核心产品团队的工作。如今大多数产品经理都无法跨团队协作，这段经历堪称产品管理的速成班，让我深刻理解了优秀PM的标准，也总结了失败案例。
发挥了重要影响力。随后，他在谷歌和YouTube担任了多个产品经理职位。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Coming back to noticing. It comes up again and again in our chat. This is so interesting because it feels like you basically came from the mail room of tech to the top of the product field. And so I think there's a lot of inspiration people can take from this journey. One quick question is how long was that journey from not being a PM, from I guess being at a tech company to getting your first PM role? Just to give people a sense.
turns.zh: 回到"洞察力"这个话题。这在我们的对话中反复出现。这很有意思，因为你似乎从科技公司的邮件收发室一路攀升至产品领域的顶端。我认为这个经历能给很多人带来启发。想快速问一下：从不做产品经理，到加入科技公司，再获得首个产品经理职位，这段历程持续了多久？让大家有个概念。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Let's see. I probably worked for at least four, five years before being able to move to PM and I think that was a slightly harrowing journey because at the time, you had to have a computer science degree.
turns.zh: 让我想想。我大概花了四五年时间才转到产品经理岗位，这段历程相当曲折，因为当时你必须拥有计算机科学学位。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: At Google. Right. Cool. So I think that's one takeaway too is give it time. It's not going to happen. There's a lot of people that are just like, "I need to become a PM immediately."
turns.zh: 在谷歌。是的。不错。所以我觉得另一个启示是耐心等待。这事急不得。很多人一心想"我必须马上成为产品经理"。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全赞同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that's a good example of it's not going to happen overnight. Coming back to your two lessons, I think they're really interesting and I'm curious if there's anything else that comes to mind of what you found was essential to you succeeding in this path? So the first lesson you shared as being customer facing. And in this case being in retail as customer facing, is your advice get in a tech company and work on something customers use or is even working at Starbucks or Abercrombie, does that count?
turns.zh: 我觉得这很好地说明了成功之路并非一蹴而就。回到你提到的两个经验教训，真的很有意思。我很好奇是否还有其他关键因素助你在这条道路上取得成功？第一个经验是以客户为导向。就零售业而言，身处客户前线岗位，你的建议是进入科技公司参与客户使用的产品开发，还是在星巴克或Abercrombie这样的零售店工作也算数？

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Yeah. I think maybe to relate it to what you just said, if I were to give advice to someone who really aspires to be a PM or trying to get into PM, I think in many cases if you're in a customer facing role, you are the expert on the customer and that is really, really valuable in tech organizations. And oftentimes it's undervalued. And so I think people who want to move into PM roles who are not currently in PM roles can often lever that experience and that knowledge of the customer in ways that are pretty profound for the organization and pretty insightful for the organization if they really are creative about it. And then I think the other thing is, regardless of where you are in the organization, you're always serving a customer. You can't just talk to one big enterprise customer and you can't just talk to the smallest customer. You have to have a diverse and continuous stream of customer interactions in order to have good intuitions about what to do next. And your engineers aren't going to really trust you unless you have good intuitions about where the customer's headed and what they want and stuff like that. And so the stakes I think are pretty high. The good news is it's easier than ever with all these tools to really get into the mindset of a customer.
turns.zh: 是的。我觉得可以结合你刚才的观点来回答。如果要给那些渴望成为产品经理或正努力进入产品经理岗位的人建议，我认为在很多情况下，如果你身处客户前线岗位，你就是客户的专家，这在科技公司中非常宝贵，却常被低估。因此，非产品经理背景的人若想转入产品经理岗位，完全可以通过创造性地利用这些客户洞察，为组织创造深刻价值。另一个关键点是，无论你在组织中处于何种位置，你始终在为客户服务。你不能只与一个大型企业客户沟通，也不能只与最微小的客户交流。你需要持续且多样化的客户互动，才能准确把握下一步行动的方向。除非你对客户的需求和偏好有深刻洞察，否则工程师们是不会真正信任你的。所以，挑战确实很大。好消息是，借助各种工具，深入理解客户需求比以往任何时候都容易。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: My lesson touches on something a previous guest talked about, Paige Costello, where she was often the youngest person in the room and built a lot of respect and people really trusted her over time. And her lesson was know thy customer. If you know the most about what they need, and you can show, here's what I've heard again and again and again, people will just like, "Oh Lane, tell us more." And they bring you into conversation because providing value, you're not just there sharing opinions. Everyone's got opinions.
turns.zh: 我的经验与前嘉宾佩奇·科斯特洛（Paige Costello）提到的相契合。她常是房间里最年轻的人，但通过持续积累尊重，最终赢得了大家的信任。她的秘诀是了解客户需求。如果你最了解他们的需求，并能展示出来，正如人们一次又一次听到的，大家会说：“哦，莱恩，多讲讲。”因为你提供的价值远不止是分享观点——每个人都有自己的观点。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: That's basically how both me and ... I had a friend named Bill Ferrell who transitioned into PM at the same time and that's essentially how we got the try at being a PM inside of Google was we knew the customer really, really well and we were often in conversations bridging the gap from here's what I think they're really saying, or here's what I think we should build based on what they said.
turns.zh: 基本上，我和……我有个朋友叫比尔·费雷尔，我们同时转型成为产品经理。实际上，我们在谷歌内部获得成为产品经理的机会，是因为我们对客户的需求非常了解，经常通过对话来缩小沟通差距。比如，我们会分析客户真正的需求，或者根据他们的反馈来规划产品功能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other thing I wanted to mention, you talked about the product and how a lot of customers don't care about the product, they just care about just I need this thing done. It reminds me at Airbnb, we hired this guy, Chip Connolly, who was a hotelier. He created the Joie de Vivre hotel chain and just is steeped in hospitality. And he came to Airbnb and started doing this worldwide tour talking to hosts. And he's just like, "Guys, when you talk about product, you're telling hosts, 'Hey, the product's going to be updated. We're going to launch all these features.', they think their home is the product of Airbnb. They don't understand what you're talking about when you're talking about the online experience and the website. That's the last thing they think about. It's the experience of someone traveling on Airbnb and staying in their home." So I think it's a really good reminder of most people don't care about the product. They just have this problem and you just happen to be this website that'll help them solve it.
turns.zh: 还有一点我想说，你提到产品经理需要关注用户需求，但很多客户并不在乎产品本身，他们只想尽快完成任务。这让我想起Airbnb的故事。我们曾聘请了酒店业资深人士奇普·康诺利，他创立了Joie de Vivre酒店集团，对酒店业有着深刻理解。他加入Airbnb后，全球巡讲与房东沟通。他发现，当你谈论产品时，房东只会想：“产品要更新啦？这些新功能什么时候上线？”他们以为自己的房源就是Airbnb的产品，而你提到的在线体验和网站改进对他们来说根本无关紧要。用户真正关心的应该是Airbnb平台上房客的体验。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: I think most people can be way more concise with their communication. Even internally, people don't care. You should assume that people don't care. Or if you're talking to customers, writing a blog post for customers, you should assume that they don't care. When you start with that assumption, you really force yourself to be a little bit sharper in your communication style.
turns.zh: 我认为大多数人本质上不关心产品，他们只想解决眼前的问题。你需要假设用户对产品并不感兴趣。即使是内部沟通，同事们也未必会仔细聆听。你得时刻保持简洁明了。面对客户时，写博客文章时，也要以用户为中心，避免复杂化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And one final question before we get to our very exciting lightning round. I heard a story that at Coda there's this moment called Tim Ferriss Day that drove a lot of traffic. Can you share that story? Does that ring a bell?
turns.zh: 在进入激动人心的闪电问答环节前，最后再问一个问题。我听说Coda有个叫“蒂姆·费里斯日”的活动，吸引了大量流量。你能分享一下这个案例吗？听起来挺耳熟的。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Yeah. There's lots of memorable days at Coda. One of them was Tim Ferris Day. So I guess maybe for context, we had built this very nascent publisher motion where we were going out and helping people publish their rituals. And this is what you see in the Coda Gallery and a lot of what we talked about today. But we had this one person on that team, this guy Al Chen, Tim Ferriss fan, and also I think had been really tenacious with the people around Tim Ferriss and basically finally got an in to him and figured out a really neat way to implement one of his rituals and wrote a doc. And so none of us really knew this, but this was all happening. And anyway, we wake up one morning and traffic is just spiking through the roof, signups are spiking, no one knows what's going on. (01:11:59): I'm convinced this is all spam. I'm like, "Something's wrong with our data or something's going haywire." At the time, we were also in the China Basin office and the fire alarm went off. And so now we're outside on our laptops. We were in a war room trying to figure out what was happening and now we're outside trying to figure out what's going on. So anyway, make a long story short, data scientists investigate and we eventually figured out that we had been featured in Tim Ferriss' email newsletter and I think early on you hear this lesson or this adage of first time founder, build a great product, second time founder, build a great distribution. I think that was one of those early big cues to think about the importance of content distribution and the importance of these publishing flywheels. And it definitely made us double down. We're like, "Okay, if we can do this with Tim Ferriss, what's next?" And we definitely spent a few months trying to reach that high watermark that was set that day in traffic and sign-ups. So it was a fun memorable day and people for the subsequent one or two years would refer to it as Tim Ferriss Day.
turns.zh: 是啊。在Coda有很多难忘的日子。其中之一就是“蒂姆·费里斯日”。所以我猜可能需要先解释一下背景，当时我们刚建立了一个新兴的出版平台，致力于帮助人们发布他们的日常仪式。这在Coda画廊里能看到，也是我们今天讨论的主要内容。但团队里有个叫阿尔·陈的成员，他是蒂姆·费里斯的粉丝，一直不懈地与蒂姆团队接触，最终成功获得了独家访问权，并想出了一个巧妙的方式来实施他的一个仪式，还写了一份文档。我们当时都不知道这些事正在发生。（01:11:59）：我当时坚信这都是垃圾邮件。我想，"我们的数据肯定出问题了，或者系统崩溃了。"那时我们还在中国湾区办公室，火警警报突然响了。于是我们就坐在外面的笔记本电脑前，原本在开战室分析情况，结果现在又要在户外继续排查故障。总之长话短说，数据科学家调查后发现，我们被列入了蒂姆·费里斯的邮件通讯。这让我想起了创业者的经验之谈：第一次创业，专注产品；第二次创业，重视分发渠道。这件事让我深刻认识到内容分发和出版飞轮的重要性，也促使我们加倍努力。我们当时想，"既然能和蒂姆·费里斯合作，那接下来该做什么？"接下来的几个月，我们一直致力于复刻那天创纪录的流量和注册量。这真是难忘的一天。接下来的一两年里，人们都称之为"蒂姆·费里斯日"。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So funny. I bet Tim Ferriss had no idea what he did.
turns.zh: 太有趣了。我敢打赌蒂姆·费里斯根本不知道自己做了什么。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: No idea.
turns.zh: 不知道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Hoping you have a Lenny's podcast day once this comes out. Everyone's going to be freaking out. What is going on here? Is there anything else you wanted to share before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 希望这期播客播出后，你也能有自己的“蒂姆·费里斯日”。大家都会兴奋不已的。这到底怎么回事？在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你还有什么想分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Maybe we're talking really briefly about two-way writeups.
turns.zh: 或许我们可以简单聊聊双向写作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, let's do it. I had that in my notes, but I skipped it, so I'm glad you mentioned it.
turns.zh: 好的，那就来吧。我之前在笔记里提到过，但跳过了，很高兴你提起了。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Cool. Yeah, I mean this is a concept that I wrote a bunch about and I often now get asked about, and I guess maybe the historical view of this, I got really obsessed with the history of how work gets discussed and decided upon and broke it down into three phases. And so the first phase was 1980s we had PowerPoint. It was this amazing tool. You could manipulate shapes on a screen and we were all using fancy clip art and it was really fun, but we've all had the experience of being in a really long PowerPoint presentation and someone's droning on in their slides and stuff like that. Second phase is in the early 2000s, two things converged. One was Google bought this company called Rightly that became Google Docs. So instead of having Word on your desktop and sending files around you now had online collaborative editing. (01:14:35): And the other thing was Jeff Bezos sent this very famous memo, which basically said no more PowerPoint at Amazon. And what that did was started in earnest their six pager ritual. You can read all about this in the book Working Backwards. It's a really good book. Colin Breyer's book. And so that started I think what I'll call the one-way writeup phase, which is you're writing down your ideas, you're expressing them clearly. It's in prose so you have to be really clear. That was a big step up I think from always presenting work and deciding on work via presentations. And then the thesis is that we're in the midst of a new phase, which is essentially two-way writeups and that's where it's more conversational and feedback and discussion is actually part of the content itself. So that's the broader historical arc. But if you think about it, PMs and product people are always at the brunt. (01:15:31): They feel this the most because they're the ones that are driving decisions and really the ones that are driving discussions oftentimes in companies. And so I think the problem with one-way writeups I felt very deeply at Google and YouTube. And just to name them, the first one is you would always be trying to figure out who's read your write-up. So I have many memories of sending a write-up out at 11:30 PM and then waiting patiently for the avatar of the SVP in my area to show up in there. And that was a sign that they had read it, which is just totally insane if you think about that behavior. The second one is you end up having a lot of the discussion in the comments itself. So this is a space that's really built for grammar and spell checking and things like that. And you're having these really meaningful discussions in this a hundred pixel right margin. (01:16:30): And part of that I think is there are all these questions that are being raised, and so you have really no idea what the most important question is. And so if you're facilitating those discussions in one way writeups, you're often going through the comments in the 20 minutes before that session trying to figure out which one of these do I want to address. And then the other behavior, and I don't know if you've ever seen this in a doc, but in one way writeups that you see a lot is there'll be just a mega comment thread on the title of the doc. And people are like, "I don't think we should do this," or you'll get into this 30 comment thread on the title because that's the best place to put your overall thoughts. And I saw this pattern all the time. So if you live that life, I think the world of two-way writeups and the way that I think a lot of our customers are doing it, and you can do this on other tools besides Coda too, I think is quite a bit better. (01:17:26): I guess the alternative to go down that list is you have a done reading button at the end of a writeup. So now you can say, oh, these are all the people that have read this. And I think even you see a pattern in some of our customers where if it's a particularly long writeup, you'll have three done reading buttons so you can see where everyone has gotten to. And then the second thing is making sure that you're actually addressing the most important question. So instead of pulling questions out of the comments and trying to figure out which one to address, just putting those in a table and then letting people upload those. And that's what we call Dory. And then I think probably the most valuable is sentiment or pulse, which is, well, how do you feel overall about this particular proposal? (01:18:13): And if you think about the contrast between a comment thread on the title and seeing a list of all the sentiment, how everybody feels about this proposal and really being inclusive to the entire audience is just wildly different. I think in my particular experience. I'll give you one example. I wrote this proposal, this is now a couple years ago. I thought it was going to sail through no problem. I thought it was going to get four out of five and five out of five smiley faces from everybody. That's sort of how the sentiment table works. And one of the lead designers basically said, "One smiley face. We shouldn't do this." And I was like, oh man. This particular person's not really vocal in meetings. And so I would not have heard that feedback. It was very unlikely I would've heard that feedback unless they had had a sentiment table, a place to add that. And so I think the punchline on all of this is I really authentically believe that this is where we're headed and hope that a lot of PMs and product teams adopt this in general.
turns.zh:
太棒了。是啊，我写过很多关于这个概念的文章，现在经常有人问起。我想从历史角度来讲，我对工作讨论和决策方式的演变特别着迷，并将其分为三个阶段。第一个阶段是1980年代，我们有了PowerPoint。这是一个很棒的工具，你可以在屏幕上操作图形，大家都用着花哨的剪贴画，玩得很开心。但我们都经历过那种冗长无聊的PowerPoint演示——讲者在幻灯片上念念叨叨的情况。

第二个阶段是21世纪初，两个因素交汇。一个是谷歌收购了Rightly公司，后来发展成Google Docs。人们不再在桌面端使用Word处理文档，而是转向在线协作编辑。（01:14:35）另一个是杰夫·贝索斯发了一份著名的备忘录，宣布亚马逊禁止使用PowerPoint。这开启了他们标志性的"六页文档"流程，详情可参阅科林·布雷耶的《Working Backwards》一书。这本书很棒。接着是"单向写作阶段"——你把想法写下来，用清晰的文字表达。这比传统的演示和决策方式有很大进步。现在我们正迈入新阶段，即"双向写作"，讨论与反馈成为内容的核心部分。

从更宏观的历史视角看，产品经理和项目经理往往首当其冲。他们在推动决策和公司讨论中发挥关键作用。我在谷歌和YouTube深有体会。单向写作的两个痛点：一是不知道谁读了你的文档。我曾深夜11点30分发送文档，焦急等待区域SVP的头像出现，确认阅读状态。二是评论区沦为讨论主场。这里本该是语法校对的地方，却承载着深度讨论。100像素的右边距实在难以容纳有意义的交流。

另一个问题是，讨论往往聚焦于标题评论区，人们用长篇大论来表达总体观点。这种行为在Coda等工具中屡见不鲜。我认为双向写作更胜一筹，许多客户正在实践这种方式。关键在于：1. 明确最重要的问题；2. 提前组织讨论焦点；3. 避免评论区沦为标题讨论的战场。
（01:17:26）：我想，处理这份阅读列表的另一种方式是在文档末尾添加一个“已完成阅读”按钮。这样一来，你就能看到所有读过这份文档的人。我相信你们中有些人也注意到，我们的客户群体中存在这样一种现象：如果一篇文章特别长，就会有三个“已完成阅读”按钮，这样你就能清楚大家读到了哪部分。第二点是确保你真正解决了最关键的问题。与其从评论中挑选问题再去思考该如何回应，不如将这些问题整理成表格，让大家自行上传。这就是我们所说的Dory功能。最有价值的功能当属情感分析或脉搏监测功能，即大家对某项提案的整体看法如何？（01:18:13）：试想一下，标题下方的评论区和展示所有参与者对该提案反馈的列表之间的对比，完全是天壤之别。在我个人经历中，我举个例子。我写的这个提案已经是几年前的事了。我原本以为它会轻松通过，得到每个人四星五星的评价。但情感分析表格显示只有一颗星，设计负责人直接说：“不能这么做。”当时我心里一沉。这位设计师平时在会议上不怎么发言，如果没有情感分析表格，我根本听不到这样的反馈。所以我认为最关键的一点是，我真心相信这就是我们未来的发展方向，希望更多的产品经理和产品团队能普遍采用这些工具。

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: Yeah. I think one thing that we've discussed before is just about strategy and planning and stuff like that. So it may be useful to touch on a couple of insights there. I think there's two insights in the strategy and planning thing. And this is again in the handbook that we're writing, but the first that I end up seeing a lot is just this idea that OKRs are not actually strategy. So I think the way that we plan and the way that our customers plan, the key point is it's critical to disconnect strategy discussions from OKR discussions. And it sounds really obvious, but it's I think a very common mistake. And I think a really simple question to ask yourself is do we have a separate strategy process or strategy ritual that is distinct from OKR setting and metric setting and goal setting? And I have found you can pick whatever strategy framework works for you, but I do think it's quite important to pull those two things apart. (01:20:43): The other rule that we live by on the planning side is what we call a 10% planning rule, which is essentially just ensure that you're not for a given time period planning for more than 10% of that execution period. And I think this is a really easy mistake to make. I mean, this is a hard fought rule because we've made that mistake before. But you end up getting bogged down in planning or saying, planning felt rushed and so we need to make it three weeks instead of one week or whatever. And the byproduct of that over the course of a lot of time is that you end up just planning way too much and oftentimes you really don't know what's ahead until you've launched or learned something. And so I think that's a pretty good rule to follow.
turns.zh: 有的。我觉得我们之前讨论过的一个点是战略和规划之类的。所以再提几点见解可能会有用。我觉得战略和规划这块有两个关键点。虽然这部分内容也在我们正在写的手册里，但我发现最常遇到的错误就是把战略讨论和OKR讨论混为一谈。关键是，要把战略讨论和OKR设定、指标设定、目标设定分开。这听起来很明显，但确实是个常见错误。一个简单的问题就是：我们有没有独立的战略流程或仪式？和OKR设定、指标设定、目标设定分开的。我觉得你可以选择任何适合你的战略框架，但分开这两件事很重要。（01:20:43）：规划方面的另一个原则是所谓的10%规划法则，就是确保在给定的时间段内，规划的时间不超过执行期的10%。这个规则来之不易，因为我们自己也犯过这个错误。但规划时往往会陷入困境，比如说规划时间太紧了，所以改成三周而不是一周之类的。长此以往，规划就过度了，往往直到产品上线或学到新东西后，才知道下一步该做什么。我觉得这条规则很值得遵循。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that rule. I found the same heuristic. 10%. If you're planning for a week, plan for half a day, planning for a month, maybe like three days. Yeah, I love it. With that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个规则。我发现了同样的启发。10%原则。比如一周的规划，半天就够。一个月的规划，三天左右。太棒了。接下来是激动人心的闪电问答环节。准备好了吗？

turns.en: You're on. That'll be our sequel. Just our game. Next question. What is a favorite life motto that you either repeat to yourself often, like to share with people around you, share with your kids maybe?
turns.zh: 我不知道这算不算座右铭，更多的是一种生活态度。本质上，当下就是我们所拥有的一切。意识到我们的注意力常常停留在过去或未来，所以当下才是它本该一直待着的地方。所以我觉得这是我经常思考的问题。我想更广泛地说，我有一位导师大致说过要让事情发生的理念，所以我真的努力把它应用到我所做的任何事情中。无论是工作、生活还是运动，我都努力成为那个能创造动力、积极改变和进步的人。所以我认为这是一个很好的生活准则。

turns.en: I don't know if it's as motto as much as it's just a way of being. It's essentially the present moment is all that we have. Realizing that our attention is very often on the past or the future and in so many ways the present is where it should be always. And so I think that that is something I think about a lot. I think maybe more broadly, I had a mentor who roughly said a version of make things happen, and so I really try to apply that to anything that I do. If that's work or life or sports, I try to be the person who creates momentum and positive change and progress. And so I think that that's generally a good motto to live by.

turns.zh: 最后一个问题。你曾在阿拉斯加做向导，帮助人们攀岩。如果有人想从事攀岩运动，有没有什么建议、经验或知识，他们应该了解，以便在攀岩之路上走得更远？

turns.en: Final question. You were a guide in Alaska helping people climb. If someone were to pursue climbing, is there a tip or a lesson or something that you think people should know to get better at this or to know before they go down this route?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。你曾在阿拉斯加做向导，帮助人们攀岩。如果有人想从事攀岩运动，有没有什么建议、经验或知识，他们应该了解，以便在攀岩之路上走得更远？

turns.speaker: Lane Shackleton
turns.en: There's a saying, which is the safest climber is the one who knows when to come down essentially. And I think that there are many times that you have to put your ego in check and come off a mountain or come out of a climb because it's not quite as safe as you thought it was. So I think that's maybe one. I think the other is it's probably not a one-way door. So I think in many ways you can do climbing and you can do some of these outdoor pursuits on the side, or you can always come back from them. So it's maybe not as big of a choice as some people think it is.
turns.zh: 有一句话说，最安全的登山者往往是知道何时该下山的人。我认为很多时候，你必须控制自己的自负情绪，从山上下来或结束攀登，因为情况可能并不像你想象的那么安全。所以我觉得这可能是第一点。另外，我认为这不一定是一条单行道。在很多方面，你可以兼职从事攀岩和其他户外运动，或者随时重新投入其中。所以这或许不像有些人想象的那么艰难的抉择。
